scenarios.title: The Overnight Overdraft
scenarios.subtitle: Concurrent Withdrawals and Lost Updates
scenarios.context:
Your team is on-call for a challenger bank's payment platform. At 02:14, PagerDuty fires: account balance monitoring reports 23 accounts with negative balances. No overdraft facility has been granted. You pull up the logs.

The system processes 2,500 withdrawal requests per second across 4 application pods. The account balance is stored in a `balance` column in PostgreSQL. The withdrawal flow is: (1) read balance, (2) check balance >= amount, (3) if yes, update balance, (4) post journal entry.

Post-mortem reveals: at peak load, 3% of accounts were overdrawn. No exceptions were logged. All transactions completed successfully from the application's perspective.
systemConstraints: 2,500 TPS peak load
4 application pods, shared PostgreSQL
READ COMMITTED isolation (default)
Withdrawal amounts: £50–£5,000
Account balances: £50–£50,000

stages.question: What is the root cause of the overnight overdrafts, and what is the most appropriate primary fix?

options.label: A
options.text: PostgreSQL connection pool exhaustion — threads are sharing connections and reading stale cached values. Fix by increasing the connection pool size and adding a connection validation query.
options.feedback: Connection pool exhaustion causes timeouts and errors — not silent overdrafts. If the pool were exhausted, withdrawals would fail with exceptions, not succeed with wrong balances. The symptom (silent wrong results) points to a race condition in the read-modify-write cycle, not a connection issue.

options.label: B
options.text: Race condition in read-modify-write cycle (lost update). Two threads both read balance=£500, both pass the check, both debit. Fix with SELECT FOR UPDATE to serialise concurrent access to the same account row.
options.feedback: Correct root cause identification. SELECT FOR UPDATE is a valid fix — it acquires an exclusive row lock at read time, forcing concurrent threads to queue. The slight deduction: SELECT FOR UPDATE serialises all concurrent access to the same account, increasing latency at high throughput. The atomic conditional UPDATE is marginally better for this workload pattern.

options.label: C
options.text: Race condition in read-modify-write cycle (lost update). Two threads both read balance=£500, both pass the check, both debit. Fix with atomic conditional UPDATE: `SET balance = balance - ? WHERE balance >= ?` — the check and debit are a single atomic operation.
options.feedback: Perfect. The root cause is a lost update: two concurrent reads both see £500, both pass the >= check, both write a reduced balance without awareness of each other. The atomic conditional UPDATE is optimal here — it eliminates the race window entirely by collapsing read-check-write into one database operation. 0 rows updated means insufficient funds; 1 row updated means success. No application-level lock needed.

options.label: D
options.text: Missing index on the accounts table is causing full table scans. Under load, table locks are promoted from row-level to table-level, causing interference between transactions. Fix by adding a covering index.
options.feedback: Index issues cause slow queries, not silent incorrect results. A table-level lock would cause timeouts and serialised access — which would actually prevent overdrafts. The symptom of parallel incorrect results with no errors is the signature of a read-modify-write race condition, not a locking/indexing issue.

stages.principalRationale: The key insight a Principal Engineer demonstrates here is distinguishing the root cause (lost update) from symptoms (overdraft), and choosing the solution that eliminates the race window entirely rather than just slowing it down. Atomic SQL is preferred over application-level locking for simple balance checks because it minimises the lock acquisition window.

stages.question: You deploy the atomic conditional UPDATE fix. Three days later, a different type of overdraft is reported: a customer's available balance showed £600, they withdrew £500, but the account was then overdrawn when a pending card authorisation of £200 settled. Under which scenario does the atomic UPDATE still produce incorrect results?

options.label: A
options.text: When network latency between the application and database exceeds 100ms, the atomic operation can be interrupted mid-execution.
options.feedback: SQL statements are atomic at the database engine level — network latency does not interrupt them once received. The database executes the UPDATE atomically regardless of how long the network round trip took. This is not a vulnerability of the atomic UPDATE approach.

options.label: B
options.text: When the balance check only uses the ledger balance but the account also maintains a separate available_balance that accounts for pending card holds. The atomic UPDATE checked ledger balance = £600, but available balance was already £400 due to the pending £200 authorisation.
options.feedback: Exactly right. The atomic UPDATE is only as correct as the balance it references. If the system has two balance concepts — ledger balance (posted transactions) and available balance (ledger minus pending holds) — the withdrawal check must use available balance. Using ledger balance ignores pending card authorisations, allowing the customer to 'spend' money already allocated to a pending debit. The fix: include reserved amounts in the WHERE clause: `WHERE (balance - reserved_amount) >= :withdrawalAmount`.

options.label: C
options.text: When more than 500 concurrent withdrawal requests target the same account simultaneously, PostgreSQL's row-level locking degrades to table-level locking, invalidating the WHERE clause evaluation.
options.feedback: PostgreSQL does not escalate row-level locks to table-level locks based on concurrency count (unlike some other databases). Row-level locking remains row-level regardless of concurrent request volume. The atomic conditional UPDATE scales well under high concurrency on the same row.

options.label: D
options.text: When the PostgreSQL isolation level is READ COMMITTED — the WHERE clause evaluation and the UPDATE write can observe different versions of the row, re-introducing the race condition.
options.feedback: This is a reasonable but incorrect concern. In PostgreSQL's READ COMMITTED, a single UPDATE statement evaluates its WHERE clause and performs the write in a single atomic operation from the row's perspective. The row is locked for the duration of the UPDATE. The race condition in the original code was between a separate SELECT and a later UPDATE — two operations. A single UPDATE statement does not have this vulnerability.

stages.principalRationale: Principal Engineers look beyond the immediate fix to understand the broader data model. 'Balance' in banking is not a single number — it has multiple representations (ledger, available, cleared, pending). The fix must reference the correct balance type for the business operation being performed.

stages.question: Both fixes are deployed. What operational metric best provides ongoing assurance that overdrafts cannot occur in production?

options.label: A
options.text: Monitor the average response time of the withdrawal endpoint. If the fix is correct, latency will remain stable and there will be no sudden spikes.
options.feedback: Response time measures performance, not financial correctness. A system can be fast and still create overdrafts. Latency monitoring is important for SLAs but provides no assurance about balance correctness.

options.label: B
options.text: Run a continuous SQL assertion: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts WHERE balance < -overdraft_limit`. Alert when count > 0. Any result above 0 indicates an unauthorised negative balance.
options.feedback: This is the correct answer. A financial invariant check that queries for the exact condition being prevented is the gold standard. It runs in production, detects actual violations as they occur, and pages the on-call engineer immediately. This is defensive engineering — verify the invariant, not just the mechanism.

options.label: C
options.text: Monitor PostgreSQL lock wait time P99. If locks are working correctly and not timing out, overdrafts cannot occur.
options.feedback: Lock wait time tells you about locking performance, but not about whether the application logic is correct. If you switched from SELECT FOR UPDATE to atomic SQL (which requires no application-level lock), there would be no lock wait time to monitor at all, yet overdrafts would still be prevented. The metric measures the mechanism, not the invariant.

options.label: D
options.text: Monitor withdrawal decline rate. If it stays below 2%, the business logic is functioning correctly and overdrafts are being prevented.
options.feedback: Decline rate measures the false-negative rate of the balance check — not the false-positive rate. The original bug was that withdrawals that should have been declined (insufficient funds) were instead approved. A correct decline rate tells you nothing about whether approved withdrawals are incorrectly draining balances below zero.

stages.principalRationale: The right operational posture for a financial invariant is to monitor the invariant directly, not to infer it from proxy metrics. 'No accounts with negative balances' is the invariant. Query for it. Alert on it. This is the difference between hoping the fix works and knowing it works.

debrief.summary: The root cause was a classic lost update — a read-modify-write cycle without atomicity guarantees. The primary fix is to make the check and the write a single atomic database operation. The deeper lesson is that 'balance' in a banking system is multi-dimensional (ledger vs available), and the check must use the correct balance type for the operation. Operational assurance comes from monitoring financial invariants directly, not performance proxies.
keyTakeaways: READ COMMITTED isolation does NOT prevent lost updates — it only prevents dirty reads
Atomic SQL (`UPDATE ... WHERE condition`) is preferred over SELECT FOR UPDATE for simple balance checks
Banking balances have multiple representations: ledger balance ≠ available balance
Monitor financial invariants directly in production: `balance < -overdraft_limit` should always return 0 rows
Principal Engineers distinguish root cause (lost update) from symptom (overdraft) and from mechanism (missing lock)

scenarios.title: The Double Charge
scenarios.subtitle: Idempotency and Duplicate Payment Detection
scenarios.context:
Customer service has escalated 50 double-charge complaints in the past week. Investigation shows: mobile app clients use an aggressive retry policy — if no response within 3 seconds, they retry up to 3 times. Under load, the payment service occasionally takes 4–6 seconds to respond.

The current idempotency implementation checks for an existing payment by idempotency key before inserting. The idempotency key is a UUID generated by the client before the first attempt.
systemConstraints: Mobile clients retry on 3-second timeout, up to 3 retries
Payment service p95 latency: 2s, p99: 5.5s under load
Idempotency key: client-generated UUID, expires after 24h
10,000 TPS peak
Microservices: Payment API → Payment Service → Ledger Service

stages.question: The current code uses: (1) SELECT payment WHERE idempotency_key = ?, (2) if found, return existing result, (3) if not found, INSERT new payment and process. What is the fundamental flaw in this approach?

options.label: A
options.text: The idempotency key should be generated server-side. Client-generated keys cannot be trusted and may collide across different clients.
options.feedback: Client-generated UUIDs are the industry standard (Stripe, Adyen, Wise all use them). UUID v4 collision probability is astronomically low. The key benefit of client-generated keys is that the client can embed the key before the first attempt and use it on all retries — if the server generates it, the client would need a separate round trip to get the key before making the payment request. This is a valid consideration but not the primary bug.

options.label: B
options.text: The SELECT and INSERT are two separate operations with a race window between them. Two concurrent retries can both pass the SELECT check (finding nothing) before either commits the INSERT. Both then insert, creating duplicate payments.
options.feedback: Exactly right. This is the check-then-act anti-pattern applied to idempotency. Under single-threaded, single-pod conditions it works fine. Under concurrent load with retries arriving simultaneously, two threads can both execute the SELECT and find no existing record, both pass the check, and both proceed to INSERT. The database commits both. The fix: delegate deduplication to the database via a UNIQUE constraint on the idempotency key column.

options.label: C
options.text: The SELECT query needs a row-level lock (SELECT FOR UPDATE) to prevent concurrent reads from seeing the same empty result.
options.feedback: SELECT FOR UPDATE on a row that doesn't exist yet cannot prevent concurrent inserts. You can only lock rows that exist. Two concurrent transactions doing SELECT FOR UPDATE on a non-existent row will both proceed and both INSERT. The lock would only help if the row already existed. The correct fix is a UNIQUE constraint — which causes one INSERT to succeed and the other to get a constraint violation, which the application handles by returning the first result.

options.label: D
options.text: The 24-hour expiry on idempotency keys is too short. Keys should be permanent to prevent customers from accidentally re-initiating payments after key expiry.
options.feedback: Key expiry length is a product decision, not a correctness bug. Permanent keys have storage implications and no clear benefit beyond 24-72 hours for retry scenarios. This does not address the double-charge problem, which occurs within seconds of the original request — well within any reasonable expiry window.

stages.principalRationale: The check-then-act pattern is a classic concurrency anti-pattern. In a distributed system with retries, the gap between check and act can be measured in microseconds — enough for a concurrent duplicate to slip through. The fix delegates atomicity to the database, which provides it natively via UNIQUE constraints.

stages.question: You replace the check-then-insert with a UNIQUE constraint on `idempotency_key`. A concurrent duplicate request triggers a DataIntegrityViolationException. What should the service return to the client?

options.label: A
options.text: HTTP 409 Conflict — the request conflicts with existing state. The client should handle this as a recoverable error.
options.feedback: HTTP 409 Conflict implies the client must take action to resolve a conflict. But there is no conflict here from the client's perspective — they just want to know if their payment went through. Returning 409 would force the client to implement special handling for a situation that is actually a success. The duplicate is handled; it is not an error.

options.label: B
options.text: HTTP 500 Internal Server Error — the UNIQUE constraint violation is an unexpected database error that should be surfaced to the client.
options.feedback: A UNIQUE constraint violation on the idempotency key is entirely expected and represents correct deduplication working as designed. Surfacing it as a 500 would cause the client to treat a successfully handled duplicate as a system failure, potentially triggering further retries and alarm. The violation must be caught and handled gracefully.

options.label: C
options.text: HTTP 200 OK with the original payment's result — look up the existing payment by idempotency key and return exactly the same response as the first successful request.
options.feedback: Correct. The duplicate constraint violation means the payment was already processed successfully. The service catches the DataIntegrityViolationException, looks up the original payment record by idempotency key, and returns its result. The client receives a consistent response: the same payment ID, amount, and status as the original. From the client's perspective, the retry behaved identically to the first request succeeding.

options.label: D
options.text: HTTP 400 Bad Request — the client sent a duplicate idempotency key, which indicates a client-side programming error.
options.feedback: Duplicate idempotency keys are intentional — they are how retries work. A client sending the same key on a retry is using the idempotency mechanism correctly, not making a programming error. HTTP 400 would penalise correct client behaviour. The client's retry with the same key is the right thing to do; the server must handle it correctly.

stages.principalRationale: Idempotency is a server-side contract: 'if you send me the same request multiple times, I will process it once and return a consistent result every time.' The constraint violation is not an error — it is the deduplication mechanism succeeding. The response to any duplicate must be identical to the response to the original.

stages.question: A retry arrives while the original payment is still in PROCESSING status (not yet committed). What is the correct response?

options.label: A
options.text: Block the retry thread until the original processing completes, then return the final result.
options.feedback: Blocking is dangerous: if the original payment is stuck (e.g., awaiting an external FX response), the retry thread blocks indefinitely. Under load, this exhausts the thread pool. The retry client will timeout again and retry again, compounding the problem. Blocking is never the right answer in an async payment flow.

options.label: B
options.text: Return HTTP 202 Accepted with a `Location` or `status_url` header pointing to a polling endpoint for the payment's current status.
options.feedback: Correct. HTTP 202 Accepted communicates: 'your request was received and is being processed — check back for the result.' The client polls the status URL periodically. This decouples the retry response from the processing duration, preventing thread exhaustion on the server and timeout loops on the client. This is the standard pattern for long-running async operations in REST APIs.

options.label: C
options.text: Process the payment a second time in parallel. If both complete, reconcile them. This ensures at-least-once processing.
options.feedback: This is the worst possible response — it deliberately creates the duplicate you are trying to prevent. 'At-least-once processing' is a valid messaging guarantee, but it requires idempotent consumers downstream. Processing the same payment twice in parallel without idempotency guarantees the duplicate the entire system is designed to prevent.

options.label: D
options.text: Return HTTP 200 OK with status=PROCESSING. The client can re-use the same idempotency key to check back.
options.feedback: Returning 200 with status=PROCESSING is reasonable but incomplete. The key improvement is to also return a polling URL (202 + Location header) so the client knows exactly where to check for the final status, rather than needing to resend the full payment request again. Without a status URL, the client must guess how to check the payment status.

stages.principalRationale: Idempotency and async processing interact here. The correct contract: if the payment is in-flight, acknowledge receipt without committing to a result yet. HTTP 202 + polling URL separates 'I received your request' from 'your payment completed'. This is robust to any duration of processing and any retry interval.

debrief.summary: Duplicate payments arise from two distinct issues: the check-then-act race (concurrent retries bypass the application check) and in-flight duplicates (retry arrives while original processes). The UNIQUE constraint fix addresses the first by delegating atomicity to the database. The 202 + polling pattern addresses the second by decoupling acknowledgement from completion.
keyTakeaways: Check-then-act is never safe for deduplication under concurrency — use UNIQUE constraints
A UNIQUE constraint violation on idempotency key is not an error — handle it and return the original result
Never return 409 Conflict for a successfully handled duplicate — return the original result
In-flight duplicates require 202 Accepted + polling, not blocking or parallel processing
Client-generated idempotency keys are the industry standard — do not replace them with server-generated keys

Track 06, Lesson 12 — Idempotency Design Patterns and Implementation

scenarios.title: The Lost Event
scenarios.subtitle: Database and Kafka Dual-Write Problem
scenarios.context:
A payment service saves a payment record to PostgreSQL and then publishes a PaymentProcessedEvent to Kafka. Downstream services (notification, analytics, AML) consume the Kafka event to trigger their workflows.

In production, 1-in-10,000 payments results in a complaint: the customer's payment was processed (money moved), but they received no confirmation notification, and the AML system has no record of the transaction. Investigation reveals: the service crashed after the PostgreSQL commit but before the Kafka publish.
systemConstraints: Payment service: Spring Boot on Kubernetes, 6 pods
Kafka: 3-broker cluster, replication factor 3
PostgreSQL: primary + 2 read replicas
Downstream consumers: notification, analytics, AML (all Kafka consumers)
Current implementation: DB commit, then Kafka produce, then HTTP 200

stages.question: What is the name of this consistency problem and what is the correct architectural fix?

options.label: A
options.text: This is eventual consistency — acceptable in distributed systems. Use a Saga pattern with compensating transactions to handle the rare cases where Kafka delivery fails.
options.feedback: The Saga pattern addresses distributed transaction failures across multiple services. It does not solve the dual-write problem: the original issue is that the payment is committed but the event is never published — there is nothing for a Saga to compensate. Eventual consistency is a valid property of distributed systems, but 'silently losing 1-in-10,000 events' is not an acceptable manifestation of it in a financial system.

options.label: B
options.text: This is the dual-write problem — writing to two different stores without atomicity between them. The fix is the Transactional Outbox Pattern: write the event to an `outbox_events` table in the same DB transaction as the payment, then have a separate poller publish from the outbox to Kafka.
options.feedback: Correct. The dual-write problem occurs when you must write to two systems (DB + Kafka) but have no cross-system transaction. The Transactional Outbox Pattern solves it by reducing the problem to a single atomic DB write: payment record + outbox event in one transaction. The poller then has the event durably stored and can retry publishing indefinitely. The event is never lost: either the transaction committed (event in outbox, guaranteed to be published eventually) or it rolled back (event never created).

options.label: C
options.text: This is an at-most-once delivery issue. Enable Kafka producer idempotence (enable.idempotence=true) and retry the produce indefinitely after a failure.
options.feedback: Kafka producer idempotence prevents duplicates when the producer retries after a network error. It does not help when the producer process crashes before making any attempt to produce. The event was never sent — it was lost in the application's in-memory state. Producer idempotence only protects against duplicate delivery, not against events never being created in the first place.

options.label: D
options.text: This is a Kafka availability issue. Add a circuit breaker: if Kafka is unavailable, buffer events in Redis and flush them when Kafka recovers.
options.feedback: Redis buffering still has the dual-write problem: you would need to atomically write to PostgreSQL and Redis. Redis also does not provide ACID guarantees equivalent to a relational database. If the process crashes after the DB commit but before the Redis write, the event is still lost. The fundamental issue is the absence of a durable, atomic write that covers both the payment and the event.

stages.principalRationale: The Transactional Outbox Pattern is the canonical solution to the dual-write problem. It leverages the ACID properties of your existing relational database to make the event creation part of the payment transaction — an indivisible operation. This is a foundational pattern in event-driven financial architectures.

stages.question: You implement the Outbox Pattern. The outbox poller reads pending events from the `outbox_events` table, publishes to Kafka, and marks the event as `published=true`. What failure mode does this architecture still have?

options.label: A
options.text: The poller may publish the same event to Kafka twice if it crashes after publishing but before marking the event as `published=true` in the database.
options.feedback: Exactly. The poller has its own two-step operation: (1) publish to Kafka, (2) mark published in DB. If the poller crashes between these two steps, it will restart, re-read the unpublished event, and publish again. This means downstream Kafka consumers can receive the same payment event multiple times. This is at-least-once delivery — a known and acceptable trade-off of the Outbox Pattern. The fix: downstream consumers must be idempotent.

options.label: B
options.text: Kafka consumers may process events out of order because the poller batches multiple events and delivers them out of sequence.
options.feedback: Event ordering is a real concern in distributed systems, but it is not specific to the Outbox Pattern and is managed by Kafka's partition assignment (all events for the same payment/account key go to the same partition, preserving order). The more fundamental vulnerability is at-least-once delivery from the poller, not ordering.

options.label: C
options.text: The outbox table becomes a performance bottleneck because every payment write now requires two inserts (payments + outbox_events) in the same transaction.
options.feedback: Two inserts in one transaction is a minor performance cost — typically sub-millisecond. It is not a bottleneck in any realistic payment processing architecture. The architectural correctness of the Outbox Pattern far outweighs this marginal performance overhead.

options.label: D
options.text: The outbox pattern breaks the ACID properties of the payment transaction because the event write is in a separate table.
options.feedback: Writing to two tables in the same database transaction is fully ACID compliant. The entire transaction (payments INSERT + outbox_events INSERT) commits atomically or rolls back atomically. This is the entire point of the Outbox Pattern: both writes are in the same transaction, in the same database, under the same ACID guarantees.

stages.principalRationale: The Outbox Pattern trades the dual-write problem for at-least-once delivery. This is an explicit, understood trade-off: events may be delivered more than once, but they will never be lost. Knowing this trade-off is essential to designing correct downstream consumers.

stages.question: Given that the outbox poller provides at-least-once delivery, what must the downstream Kafka consumer do to maintain exactly-once processing semantics?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable Kafka Streams exactly-once processing (processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2) on the consumer side.
options.feedback: Kafka Streams exactly-once semantics (EOS) provides transactional guarantees within Kafka Streams applications — consuming from one topic and producing to another atomically. For consuming and writing to a database (the common case in payment processing), EOS alone does not help. The consumer must use application-level idempotency to handle duplicate events from the outbox.

options.label: B
options.text: Be idempotent: use the payment's unique ID as an idempotency key when processing the event. If the event was already processed (record exists with that payment ID), skip processing and acknowledge the message.
options.feedback: Correct. Idempotent consumers are the complement to at-least-once delivery. The consumer stores a record of processed payment IDs (via a UNIQUE constraint in its own database or a Redis set). On each event, it checks whether this payment ID has been processed. If yes: acknowledge the Kafka message and skip. If no: process and record. This combination of at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumer achieves effective exactly-once business semantics.

options.label: C
options.text: Reject duplicate Kafka messages at the consumer by checking the message offset. If the offset was already processed, discard it.
options.feedback: Kafka offsets are per-partition and per-consumer-group. After a consumer group rebalance or restart, the same offset is not reused — but the same message content (same payment ID) may arrive from a different offset due to the outbox poller publishing it twice. Offset-based deduplication only prevents replays within a continuous consumer session, not across restarts or redeliveries from the outbox.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a distributed lock (Redis SETNX keyed on payment ID) for the duration of event processing. If the lock is already held, the duplicate is discarded.
options.feedback: Distributed locks add complexity and a dependency on Redis availability. If Redis is unavailable, payment processing halts. The UNIQUE constraint approach is simpler, more reliable, and directly in the application's primary data store. Locks are appropriate for time-bounded operations; idempotency checks are appropriate for deduplication.

stages.principalRationale: At-least-once delivery + idempotent consumers = effective exactly-once business semantics. This combination is used by Stripe, Wise, and virtually every production-grade payment system. The pattern is: (1) accept that messages may arrive more than once, (2) design consumers to handle duplicates gracefully using unique business keys.

debrief.summary: The dual-write problem is fundamental to event-driven architectures. The Transactional Outbox Pattern solves it by making event creation part of the database transaction. The price is at-least-once delivery from the poller — which requires idempotent consumers. This three-layer solution (DB transaction + outbox + idempotent consumers) is the production-grade pattern for consistent event publishing.
keyTakeaways: Dual-write (DB + Kafka) without atomicity means you can commit to one but not the other
The Transactional Outbox Pattern makes event creation part of the DB transaction — events are never lost
The outbox poller provides at-least-once delivery — it may publish the same event twice
Downstream consumers must be idempotent using business keys (payment ID), not Kafka offsets
Kafka producer idempotence prevents duplicate delivery but not events never created in the first place

scenarios.title: The Hot Account
scenarios.subtitle: Concurrent Balance Updates at Scale
scenarios.context:
A UK challenger bank handles HMRC (tax authority) payroll credit runs: 3 million employees' salaries paid via BACS within a 2-hour window. This routes through a single HMRC suspense account at the bank that receives 3,000 credits and debits per second.

The current implementation uses SELECT FOR UPDATE on the account row for every transaction. Under this load, p99 latency for account updates has reached 8 seconds. The lock queue depth grows to 1,200 waiting transactions. Transactions are timing out at the application layer, causing retries that further amplify the problem.
systemConstraints: 3,000 TPS on a single account (HMRC suspense)
Lock queue depth: 1,200 waiting transactions
p99 latency: 8 seconds (SLA: 500ms)
Exact balance must be maintained at all times (regulatory)
Downstream systems consume balance-change events

stages.question: SELECT FOR UPDATE is creating an 8-second lock queue at 3,000 TPS. What architectural change provides the highest throughput while maintaining exact balance correctness?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase PostgreSQL max_connections and application connection pool size to handle more concurrent waiters in the lock queue.
options.feedback: More connections means more threads waiting for the same lock. The bottleneck is the lock contention on the single account row, not the number of connection slots available. Adding more waiting threads increases memory pressure and context switching overhead without reducing the fundamental serialisation. The lock queue would grow from 1,200 to a larger number — still resulting in multi-second latency.

options.label: B
options.text: Replace SELECT FOR UPDATE with optimistic locking (@Version). Under low conflict, optimistic locking eliminates lock wait time. Retries on conflict handle the rare cases.
options.feedback: Optimistic locking works well when conflicts are rare. At 3,000 TPS on a single account, virtually every update will conflict with another. The retry rate approaches 100%, meaning every transaction retries multiple times before succeeding. Under high contention, optimistic locking performs worse than pessimistic locking because retried transactions waste work: they read, check, fail, re-read, re-check, and re-attempt — multiplying database load.

options.label: C
options.text: Route all writes to the HMRC account through a single dedicated async queue with one consumer that serialises updates sequentially. The queue provides back-pressure and predictable throughput. The consumer can batch nearby updates (e.g., 100ms windows) for improved efficiency.
options.feedback: Correct. Queue-based serialisation is the correct pattern for hot account access. By funnelling all writes through a queue, the serial access constraint is maintained but the database lock is replaced with an in-memory queue — orders of magnitude faster. Batching within the consumer further multiplies throughput: a single DB transaction can apply 50-100 balance updates, dramatically reducing DB round trips. This is how payment systems like Stripe handle hot merchant accounts.

options.label: D
options.text: Shard the account balance into 10 'sub-balances'. Distribute writes across sub-balances. Compute total balance by summing all 10 sub-balances when needed.
options.feedback: Balance sharding (similar to CRDTs / G-Counters) is a valid high-throughput approach that eliminates hot-account contention entirely. The trade-off is that the 'true' balance at any instant requires an aggregate query across all shards — which is not guaranteed to reflect in-flight transactions. For a suspense account with strict regulatory balance requirements (exact balance must be known at any point), this eventual consistency is typically unacceptable. Queue serialisation maintains exact consistency.

stages.principalRationale: Queue-based serialisation converts a database locking problem into an in-memory queuing problem. Lock queues in a database are expensive — each waiter holds a connection, and context switching between DB processes is costly. An in-memory queue is hundreds of times cheaper per waiter. The serial access requirement is preserved; only the mechanism changes.

stages.question: You deploy queue-based serialisation with one consumer. During a Kubernetes rolling deployment, the queue consumer pod is briefly unavailable. The queue depth grows to 50,000 events in 90 seconds. What design prevents this single point of failure while maintaining serial balance updates?

options.label: A
options.text: Run 3 consumer replicas. Use Kafka consumer group assignment to distribute events across replicas for parallel processing.
options.feedback: Multiple consumers in the same consumer group processing different partitions works for independent events, but all HMRC account balance events must be serialised. If 3 consumers process events in parallel, you re-introduce the race condition you eliminated. Parallel consumers defeat the purpose of queue serialisation for a single account.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Kafka partitioning keyed on account ID. All events for the HMRC account always go to the same partition. Run multiple consumer replicas — only one will be assigned the HMRC account partition. If that replica fails, the partition is rebalanced to another replica within seconds.
options.feedback: Correct. Account-keyed partitioning guarantees that all events for the same account always flow through the same consumer at any point in time. During a rebalance, the partition is reassigned to another replica — there is a brief pause (seconds) but no race condition and no data loss. This is the standard pattern for hot-key processing in Kafka-based financial systems. Add a cold standby partition for the HMRC account for sub-second failover.

options.label: C
options.text: Fall back to SELECT FOR UPDATE during queue consumer unavailability. Detect the outage via health check and switch to database locking mode automatically.
options.feedback: A fallback to SELECT FOR UPDATE is a reasonable defence-in-depth measure. It maintains correctness during outages. However, the lock queue problem will immediately recur at 3,000 TPS. The fallback buys time but is not a sustainable operating mode. The primary fix should ensure the queue consumer is highly available rather than relying on the fallback.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the Kafka consumer's max.poll.records to 10,000 to drain the backlog faster when the consumer recovers.
options.feedback: Increasing batch size helps drain a backlog faster after recovery, but does not prevent the SPOF problem during the outage. The question asks how to prevent the single point of failure — the core issue is that one consumer pod failing means zero processing. The fix is high availability via partition rebalancing, not faster batch processing.

stages.principalRationale: Kafka's partition-per-key model is exactly designed for this use case. It guarantees that one and only one consumer processes events for a given key at any time, while allowing fast failover when that consumer fails. This is a core pattern for maintaining consistency and high availability simultaneously.

stages.question: The queue consumer batches 100ms windows of events into single DB transactions. This improves throughput from 500 TPS to 8,000 TPS. What consistency guarantee does this batching sacrifice?

options.label: A
options.text: No consistency guarantee is sacrificed — batching only improves performance. ACID properties are fully maintained because all events in a batch commit together.
options.feedback: Partial credit. It is true that the batch commit is ACID compliant. However, batching does sacrifice real-time balance visibility: during the 100ms window, the account balance in the database reflects the state before the batch, not the in-flight events. Any read of the balance during this window sees a stale balance. For regulatory reporting that requires real-time balance accuracy, this is a meaningful consistency degradation.

options.label: B
options.text: Real-time balance visibility — during the 100ms batching window, the database balance does not reflect in-flight events in the queue. Any query of the account balance returns a value that is up to 100ms stale.
options.feedback: Correct. Batching introduces a commit latency: the account balance in the database lags the queue by up to the batch window (100ms). Any balance inquiry during that window returns a stale value. For the HMRC use case with regulatory requirements for exact real-time balance, this may require the consumer to maintain an in-memory 'working balance' that includes uncommitted queue events, available for queries via a separate read path.

options.label: C
options.text: Durability — events in the 100ms batch window may be lost if the consumer crashes before the batch commits.
options.feedback: Durability is preserved by Kafka: uncommitted batch events remain in the Kafka topic and will be reprocessed when the consumer restarts. The consumer uses manual offset commit — only committing Kafka offsets after the DB transaction commits. A crash before commit leaves the offsets uncommitted and the events will be redelivered. Durability is not sacrificed by batching when combined with correct offset management.

options.label: D
options.text: Atomicity — events in the same 100ms window may be partially applied if the DB transaction rolls back midway through the batch.
options.feedback: If the DB transaction for a batch rolls back, all events in the batch are rolled back together. None are partially applied. Kafka offsets are only committed after a successful DB commit, so the batch will be reprocessed from the first uncommitted event. Atomicity is preserved by the DB transaction boundary.

stages.principalRationale: Every performance optimisation in distributed systems trades something. Batching trades commit latency for throughput. For financial balances, the trade-off must be explicitly understood and mitigated (e.g., in-memory working balance for queries). Principal Engineers name the trade-offs precisely rather than claiming 'no trade-off'.

debrief.summary: The hot account problem is caused by SELECT FOR UPDATE serialising all access to a single row — correct for correctness, catastrophic for throughput at scale. Queue-based serialisation moves the serialisation point from the database to an in-memory queue, achieving orders-of-magnitude throughput improvement. Kafka partitioning by account key provides high availability. Batching within the consumer multiplies throughput further, at the cost of real-time balance visibility.
keyTakeaways: SELECT FOR UPDATE serialises correctly but cannot scale beyond ~100-200 TPS on a single row
Queue-based serialisation achieves serial access without DB locks — thousands of TPS per account
Kafka partition-per-key guarantees exactly-one-consumer-per-account for correctness + high availability
Batching in the consumer dramatically improves throughput at the cost of commit latency
Name the trade-offs explicitly: 'batching sacrifices real-time balance visibility up to 100ms'

scenarios.title: The Failed Saga
scenarios.subtitle: Partial Payment Failure and Compensation
scenarios.context:
A cross-border payment flow consists of three steps executed across three microservices: (1) FX Service — quote and lock an exchange rate, (2) Debit Service — debit the customer's GBP account, (3) Credit Service — credit the beneficiary's USD account.

In production, step 3 (Credit) fails 0.3% of the time due to the beneficiary bank's API returning 503 errors. Currently, the system logs the failure and alerts. The GBP debit has already been posted. The customer's money is debited but never arrives at the destination.
systemConstraints: Three independent microservices: FX, Debit, Credit
No distributed transaction (no 2PC) — each service has its own database
Step 3 failure rate: 0.3% (beneficiary bank 503s)
Regulatory requirement: a failed payment must fully reverse within 24 hours
FX rate lock expires in 60 seconds

stages.question: Steps 1 and 2 have succeeded. Step 3 (Credit) fails with a 503 from the beneficiary bank. What is the correct architectural response to maintain financial consistency?

options.label: A
options.text: Introduce a distributed two-phase commit (2PC/XA) across all three services. If step 3 fails, the XA coordinator rolls back steps 1 and 2 automatically.
options.feedback: 2PC is technically possible but practically problematic in microservices. It requires a distributed coordinator (e.g., XA Resource Manager), all three services and databases to support XA, and holds locks across all services during the commit phase — potentially for seconds. A 503 from the beneficiary bank (which may take 30 seconds to timeout) would hold all three locks for 30 seconds. Under high volume, this creates catastrophic lock contention. The industry consensus: use Sagas, not 2PC, in microservices architectures.

options.label: B
options.text: Implement a Saga with compensating transactions: if step 3 fails, the Saga orchestrator triggers step 2-reversal (reverse the GBP debit) and step 1-release (release the FX rate lock). Financial state is returned to pre-payment condition.
options.feedback: Correct. The Saga pattern is the standard approach for distributed transactions in microservices. When step 3 fails, the Saga executes compensating transactions in reverse order: reverse the debit (re-credit the customer's GBP), then release the FX lock. Because each step and its compensating action are designed idempotently, the Saga can safely retry compensation steps. The final state is consistent: either all three steps committed, or all effects are reversed.

options.label: C
options.text: Retry step 3 indefinitely with exponential backoff. If the beneficiary bank is temporarily unavailable, retrying will eventually succeed without needing to roll back.
options.feedback: Retry with exponential backoff is correct as the first line of defence — most 503 errors are transient. However, 'indefinitely' is not a production-safe policy. If the beneficiary bank is down for 24+ hours, the customer's money is frozen in limbo indefinitely. The correct policy: retry for a reasonable duration (e.g., 30 minutes with exponential backoff), then escalate to Saga compensation. Retry alone is not sufficient.

options.label: D
options.text: Let the payment remain in PARTIALLY_COMPLETE state. Queue it for manual review by operations. The operations team will decide whether to retry or refund.
options.feedback: Manual review is a valid last resort but not an architectural solution. At 0.3% failure rate and significant payment volume, manual review becomes a bottleneck and introduces human error. Regulatory requirements also typically mandate automated reversal timelines. PARTIALLY_COMPLETE state must trigger automated compensating action, not just an alert.

stages.principalRationale: The Saga pattern decomposes a distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with a corresponding compensating transaction. It trades atomicity for availability — there is a brief period where the state is inconsistent (steps 1 and 2 committed, step 3 not). But the eventual consistency guarantee (either fully committed or fully reversed) is maintained.

stages.question: The Saga triggers the compensating transaction (reverse the GBP debit). The Debit Service's compensation step itself fails: the service returns HTTP 500 (the service is restarting). The Saga orchestrator cannot complete the reversal. What must happen next?

options.label: A
options.text: Mark the Saga as FAILED and alert the on-call engineer. The engineer will manually trigger the compensation when the Debit Service recovers.
options.feedback: Alerting is essential but not sufficient. Manual intervention is slow and error-prone. If the engineer is unavailable or the alert is missed, the customer's money remains debited indefinitely. The Saga must be persisted in COMPENSATING state and retried automatically — with an alert as the escalation path if retries exhaust, not as the primary recovery mechanism.

options.label: B
options.text: Persist the Saga in COMPENSATING state with the failed step recorded. Retry the compensation with exponential backoff until it succeeds. Alert operations if compensation has not completed within the regulatory window (e.g., 1 hour). Never silently absorb a compensation failure.
options.feedback: Correct. Compensation failures are a known failure mode — the Saga literature calls these 'non-retryable' vs 'retriable' failures. For retriable failures (service temporarily down), retry with backoff until recovery. For non-retriable failures (data integrity error), escalate immediately. The key principle: a Saga stuck in COMPENSATING state is a financial emergency — persistent state + retry + alert is the correct triad.

options.label: C
options.text: Roll back the entire Saga by issuing a compensating transaction for step 1 (FX lock) only, and accept that the GBP debit cannot be reversed until the Debit Service recovers.
options.feedback: Partial rollback (reverting some steps but not others) leaves the system in an inconsistent state: the FX lock is released but the GBP debit remains. The customer has been charged but neither the payment nor the reversal has completed. Partial rollback must be avoided — the Saga must complete all compensating transactions before it can be considered resolved.

options.label: D
options.text: Issue a double-credit (credit the customer's account twice) to compensate for the failed debit reversal. The net effect will be the same as a successful reversal.
options.feedback: A double-credit would corrupt the double-entry ledger. The correct compensating transaction for a debit is a credit of the same amount — not two credits. Financial compensating transactions must be exact mirrors of the original transaction, not approximations.

stages.principalRationale: Compensation failures are not unexpected edge cases — they are a core part of Saga design. Every compensation step must be idempotent and retriable. The Saga state machine must persist the COMPENSATING state and retry indefinitely until success, with escalation on timeout. 'Fire and forget' compensation is a production disaster waiting to happen.

stages.question: Three weeks post-deployment, there are 12 Sagas stuck in COMPENSATING state for more than 2 hours each. How do you detect and alert on these in production?

options.label: A
options.text: Review the Saga state table manually during weekly engineering reviews. If more than 5 Sagas are stuck, trigger a hotfix.
options.feedback: Weekly manual reviews are not acceptable for a financial system. A Saga stuck for 2 hours means a customer's money is frozen for 2 hours. At regulatory timescales (24-hour reversal requirement), 2 hours is not critical yet, but 7 days between reviews creates unacceptable risk. Financial monitoring must be continuous and automated.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a Micrometer gauge: `EM.Lab.sagas.stuck.count` that counts Sagas with state=COMPENSATING and last_updated > 30 minutes ago. Alert via PagerDuty when count > 0 for more than 5 minutes.
options.feedback: Correct. This is exactly right. A Micrometer (or Prometheus) gauge that queries the Saga state table every minute for Sagas stuck in COMPENSATING beyond the expected recovery window, combined with a PagerDuty alert, provides real-time visibility. The 5-minute alert delay prevents noise from transient failures that resolve quickly. This is production-grade financial monitoring.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Kafka consumer lag as a proxy: if the saga orchestrator's input topic has high lag, Sagas may be backing up.
options.feedback: Kafka consumer lag indicates that the orchestrator is behind in processing new Saga commands. It does not reveal anything about the internal state of Sagas already being orchestrated. A Saga stuck in COMPENSATING may have no Kafka events associated with it after the initial failure — it is simply waiting for a service to recover. Consumer lag is an irrelevant proxy metric here.

options.label: D
options.text: Set a database-level constraint: Sagas cannot remain in COMPENSATING state for more than 60 minutes. If the timeout fires, the row is automatically deleted.
options.feedback: Automatically deleting a Saga in COMPENSATING state would destroy the record of an in-flight financial correction. The customer's debit is still posted. Deleting the Saga means there is no record of the ongoing reversal — the money is gone with no trace. This is the worst possible action. Saga records must be retained until compensation completes or is explicitly resolved by a human.

stages.principalRationale: Financial invariants must be monitored continuously with automated alerts. A Micrometer gauge that queries the Saga state table is the right tool: it queries the source of truth (the database), it surfaces the exact condition you care about (stuck in COMPENSATING), and it pages the on-call engineer in time to meet regulatory reversal windows.

debrief.summary: The Saga pattern decomposes distributed transactions into local transactions with compensating actions. It achieves eventual consistency rather than atomicity — there is always a brief window of inconsistency. The correct Saga implementation requires: idempotent compensation steps, persistent Saga state, automatic retry on transient failures, and real-time monitoring for Sagas stuck in COMPENSATING state.
keyTakeaways: 2PC in microservices is a theoretical solution — Sagas are the practical production pattern
Compensation failures are expected — Sagas must persist COMPENSATING state and retry automatically
Never silently absorb a compensation failure — it means a customer's money is in limbo
Saga stuck in COMPENSATING > 30 minutes = financial emergency requiring PagerDuty alert
Monitor the Saga state table directly with a Micrometer gauge — not Kafka lag or log parsing
furtherReading: Track 06, Lesson 06 — Scenario E: Partial Payment Failure and Compensation
Track 06, Lesson 14 — Saga Pattern: Distributed Transaction Management
Track 06, Lesson 15 — Two-Phase Commit vs Saga: When to Use Each

scenarios.title: The Cascading Timeout
scenarios.subtitle: Thread Pool Exhaustion and Cascading Failure
scenarios.context:
Your payment authorisation service calls three downstream services on every request: FraudCheck (200ms avg), BIC Validation (50ms avg), and Account Lookup (30ms). The service runs with a shared thread pool of 200 threads and processes 1,800 requests/second.

At 11:23, FraudCheck begins responding slowly — P99 climbs from 200ms to 8 seconds over 10 minutes. At 11:34, PagerDuty fires: payment authorisation service health check failing. All 200 threads are blocked waiting on FraudCheck responses. BIC Validation and Account Lookup — both healthy — are receiving zero traffic. The entire payment service is down because one downstream dependency degraded.
systemConstraints: 1,800 req/s peak throughput
Shared thread pool: 200 threads
Three downstream dependencies: FraudCheck, BIC Validation, Account Lookup
FraudCheck timeout: 30 seconds (not yet triggered at 11:34)
No circuit breakers configured
Spring MVC with blocking I/O

stages.question: What is the root cause of the complete service outage, and what architectural pattern was missing?

options.label: A
options.text: Network bandwidth saturation — FraudCheck's slow responses are consuming all available network capacity, starving BIC Validation and Account Lookup of bandwidth.
options.feedback: Slow responses consume threads, not bandwidth. A slow service holding connections open uses negligible bandwidth while blocking a thread. The failure mode is thread exhaustion, not bandwidth saturation. If this were bandwidth, all three downstream calls would degrade proportionally.

options.label: B
options.text: Thread pool exhaustion via cascade: 200 threads each blocked on a slow FraudCheck call (8s response, 1,800 req/s inflow). With a shared pool, FraudCheck's degradation consumes all threads. BIC Validation and Account Lookup are healthy but unreachable. The missing pattern is a Bulkhead: separate, bounded thread pools per downstream dependency.
options.feedback: Exactly right. This is the classic cascading failure via shared resource. At 1,800 req/s with an 8s FraudCheck response, threads accumulate at 1,800 × 8 = 14,400 blocked threads demanded — far exceeding the 200-thread pool. The bulkhead pattern isolates downstream dependencies into separate thread pools (e.g., FraudCheck: 60 threads, BIC: 20 threads, Account: 20 threads, general: 100 threads) so that FraudCheck exhausting its pool cannot affect BIC Validation requests.

options.label: C
options.text: FraudCheck is consuming too much CPU on the payment service host, starving other threads of processing time.
options.feedback: Waiting threads (blocked on I/O) do not consume CPU — they are parked by the OS scheduler. The payment service pods would show near-zero CPU utilisation while completely unresponsive. This is the counter-intuitive nature of I/O-bound thread exhaustion: the service appears idle from a CPU perspective but is completely stuck.

options.label: D
options.text: The 30-second timeout on FraudCheck is too long. Reducing it to 500ms would prevent thread exhaustion.
options.feedback: Reducing the timeout helps but is insufficient alone. With a 500ms timeout at 1,800 req/s, threads still accumulate at 1,800 × 0.5 = 900 blocked threads demanded, still far exceeding 200. Without a bulkhead, any timeout value that permits more than 200 concurrent inflight FraudCheck requests will exhaust the shared pool. Timeout tuning is necessary but not sufficient — isolation is required.

stages.principalRationale: The key insight is that a shared resource (thread pool) makes all downstream dependencies interdependent. One slow dependency can starve all others regardless of their health. The bulkhead pattern creates blast radius containment: each dependency gets its own bounded pool, so FraudCheck degradation cannot affect Account Lookup availability.

stages.question: You implement bulkhead isolation. FraudCheck is now allocated a dedicated pool of 60 threads with a 1-second timeout. During the next FraudCheck degradation, payment service stays up but 60% of payments are declined with FRAUD_CHECK_TIMEOUT errors. The business wants degraded-mode operation: skip FraudCheck and approve low-risk transactions when FraudCheck is unavailable. What is the correct implementation?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a try-catch around the FraudCheck call. On timeout, approve the transaction and log a warning.
options.feedback: Catching the timeout and approving is the right general direction, but implementing it with a bare try-catch bypasses the circuit breaker's open/half-open state machine. Without a circuit breaker, every request still attempts a FraudCheck call and waits for the timeout before falling back. At 60 threads and 1,800 req/s, the bulkhead saturates within 33ms. The fallback must be circuit-breaker-gated to avoid all 60 threads timing out.

options.label: B
options.text: Circuit breaker on the FraudCheck bulkhead with a fallback: when the breaker is OPEN (triggered by 5 failures in 10s), route to a local risk model that approves transactions with known-good customer profiles and amounts < £500. Log all fallback decisions for retrospective FraudCheck review.
options.feedback: Correct. The circuit breaker transitions CLOSED → OPEN after the failure threshold, immediately stopping new FraudCheck calls (no more thread blocking). The fallback provides a degraded-but-operational mode. The local risk model + amount ceiling limits fraud exposure during the degradation window. Logging fallback decisions for retrospective review is essential for regulatory compliance — you must demonstrate that every transaction was risk-assessed, even if the assessment was deferred.

options.label: C
options.text: Increase the FraudCheck bulkhead to 120 threads so more concurrent requests can be in-flight before saturation.
options.feedback: Increasing the bulkhead size delays saturation but does not eliminate it. It also allows more memory consumption from blocked threads. Without a circuit breaker and fallback, the eventual outcome is identical — just delayed. When FraudCheck is down, the correct response is to stop calling it quickly (circuit breaker) and fall back gracefully, not to increase the blast radius of each failure.

options.label: D
options.text: Move FraudCheck to an asynchronous model: publish a payment event to Kafka, let FraudCheck consume it and publish a decision. The authorisation waits up to 500ms for the decision event before defaulting to approve.
options.feedback: Async Kafka-mediated FraudCheck is a valid architectural pattern for high-throughput screening but introduces significant complexity: Kafka partition ordering, consumer group management, correlation ID matching between request and response events. For a synchronous authorisation path with sub-200ms SLO, an async model with a 500ms Kafka round trip would consistently breach the SLO. Address the resilience problem with a circuit breaker + local fallback before rearchitecting the communication pattern.

stages.principalRationale: The circuit breaker's OPEN state eliminates the timeout wait — calls fail immediately instead of waiting 1 second. This is the difference between graceful degradation and continued thread saturation at a slower rate. The fallback's scope (amount ceiling + known profile) bounds the financial risk of operating without FraudCheck.

stages.question: What single metric best provides ongoing assurance that bulkhead isolation is working correctly in production?

options.label: A
options.text: Monitor the payment service's overall P99 latency. If bulkheads are working, latency will remain stable during downstream degradation.
options.feedback: Overall P99 is a lagging indicator — it only confirms the bulkhead worked after the fact. It also does not distinguish between bulkhead saturation and other latency causes. You need a metric that shows bulkhead utilisation before saturation, not one that proves saturation already occurred.

options.label: B
options.text: Monitor bulkhead thread pool utilisation per dependency (active threads / pool size). Alert when any single bulkhead exceeds 80% utilisation for more than 30 seconds — this indicates imminent saturation and allows preemptive circuit breaker configuration.
options.feedback: Correct. Per-bulkhead utilisation is the leading indicator. At 80% utilisation on FraudCheck's 60-thread pool (48 active threads), you have headroom before saturation and time to investigate. At 100% utilisation, every new request is queued or rejected. This metric surfaces degradation before it becomes an outage, allowing proactive response (tighten the timeout, open the circuit breaker manually) rather than reactive firefighting.

options.label: C
options.text: Monitor the FraudCheck service's response time directly. If it exceeds 500ms, trigger an alert.
options.feedback: Monitoring FraudCheck's response time is useful but monitors the dependency, not your isolation. If your bulkhead is correctly isolating FraudCheck degradation, you care about whether the isolation is holding, not just whether FraudCheck is slow. Bulkhead utilisation gives you both: it confirms FraudCheck is degraded (threads filling up) AND shows whether the isolation boundary is approaching breach.

options.label: D
options.text: Monitor the circuit breaker state transitions. Alert when any circuit breaker transitions from CLOSED to OPEN.
options.feedback: Circuit breaker state transition alerting is valuable but is a reactive metric — the transition to OPEN means the failure threshold was already exceeded. For ongoing assurance that the architecture is working correctly, you need proactive bulkhead utilisation monitoring that shows you approaching the problem, plus the circuit breaker alert as the escalation trigger.

stages.principalRationale: Per-bulkhead utilisation is a leading indicator. It surfaces 'FraudCheck is degraded and my isolation is absorbing it' before it becomes 'FraudCheck has saturated its pool and fallback is active'. Financial systems need leading indicators, not just trailing ones.

debrief.summary: Cascading failure via shared resources is one of the most common causes of total service outage. The solution is defence-in-depth: bulkhead isolation prevents propagation; circuit breakers prevent retry storms; fallback logic maintains degraded operation. Each layer handles a different failure mode.
keyTakeaways: Shared thread pools make all downstream dependencies interdependent — one slow service can take down everything
Bulkhead pattern: separate bounded thread pools per downstream dependency
Circuit breaker eliminates the timeout wait when a service is down — fail fast, not slowly
Fallback must be designed with business risk in mind — what can you safely approve without full fraud screening?
Monitor bulkhead utilisation as a leading indicator, not overall P99 as a trailing one
furtherReading: Track 08, Lesson 03 — Circuit Breakers and Bulkheads
Track 02, Lesson 09 — Failure Isolation Patterns
Track 04, Lesson 08 — Reactive Streams and Backpressure

scenarios.title: The Kafka Rebalance Storm
scenarios.subtitle: Consumer Group Rebalance Loop Halting AML Processing
scenarios.context:
Your AML transaction monitoring system consumes from the Kafka topic `transactions.completed` (24 partitions, 3 consumer pods). To handle growing volume, the team deploys 8 additional consumer pods, expecting a 3.6× throughput increase.

Instead, within 2 minutes of deployment, all consumers begin rebalancing in a continuous loop. Kafka consumer group lag grows from near-zero to 2.3 million records. No AML alerts are generated. The monitoring dashboard shows consumers joining and leaving the group every 45 seconds. After 20 minutes, the team rolls back but the lag remains.
systemConstraints: 24 Kafka partitions, topic: transactions.completed
Original: 3 consumer pods (8 partitions each)
After scale-up: 11 consumer pods
max.poll.interval.ms: 300000 (5 minutes)
max.poll.records: 500
AML rule evaluation: calls OFAC API (avg 350ms), Redis feature store (avg 15ms)
Transactions volume: 45,000/minute

stages.question: What is causing the continuous rebalance loop, and why did it not manifest with the original 3 pods?

options.label: A
options.text: 11 consumer pods exceeds the 24 partitions / 2 minimum threshold. Kafka does not support more consumers than a fixed ratio to partitions, causing group coordinator instability.
options.feedback: Kafka supports up to N consumers per N partitions — excess consumers simply sit idle. Having 11 consumers for 24 partitions is valid; 11 would be active and 0 idle (since 11 < 24). There is no ratio threshold. The instability has a different cause.

options.label: B
options.text: Each consumer polls 500 records. With 8 partitions assigned (after rebalance), processing 500 records × 350ms OFAC call = 175 seconds per poll cycle, far exceeding max.poll.interval.ms of 300 seconds (5 minutes). With the original 3 pods (8 partitions each), it was borderline. With 11 pods (2-3 partitions each at peak lag), fewer partitions means fewer records per poll but the lag burst triggers poll batches of 500 records each with the same processing time. The key: lag burst on scale-up means every consumer immediately polls 500 records, each taking 175s — exceeding the 300s limit.
options.feedback: Correct. max.poll.interval.ms is the maximum time between consecutive poll() calls. If processing 500 records takes longer than 5 minutes, Kafka considers the consumer dead and triggers a rebalance. The rebalance causes the consumer to rejoin, which polls another 500 records at the lag peak, which again takes > 5 minutes — the loop is self-sustaining. With 3 pods at steady state, the lag was low and each poll grabbed fewer records (Kafka delivers up to max.poll.records but often fewer at low lag). The scale-up was attempted precisely because lag was growing — worst possible timing.

options.label: C
options.text: The Kafka group coordinator has a bug when more than 10 consumers join simultaneously. The coordinator enters a failed state and continuously triggers rebalances.
options.feedback: Kafka group coordinator handles arbitrarily large consumer groups and simultaneous joins correctly. Rolling restarts or gradual scale-ups are preferred for operational reasons, but the protocol supports simultaneous joins. The rebalance loop has a configuration root cause, not a Kafka coordinator bug.

options.label: D
options.text: The OFAC API has a rate limit of 100 req/s. With 11 consumers × 500 records each calling OFAC simultaneously, the rate limit is breached, causing timeouts. Timeouts extend processing time beyond max.poll.interval.ms.
options.feedback: OFAC rate limiting is a plausible contributing factor but not the primary cause described. The core issue is a configuration-driven poll interval breach. Even without rate limiting, 500 records × 350ms average = 175 seconds per batch exceeds the 300-second max.poll.interval.ms under sustained lag conditions.

stages.principalRationale: max.poll.interval.ms is one of the most misunderstood Kafka consumer settings. It is not about network heartbeats (that is heartbeat.interval.ms) — it is about the time between application-level poll() calls. Long processing batches routinely breach it in services that do synchronous external calls per record.

stages.question: After rolling back to 3 pods, lag is at 2.3M records. What is the correct strategy to drain the lag without triggering duplicate AML alerts?

options.label: A
options.text: Reset consumer offsets to the latest position (skip the lag). AML monitoring will resume from the current point; the 2.3M records are lost but can be reprocessed in a separate batch job.
options.feedback: Skipping lag means 2.3M transactions are never AML-screened in real time. For regulatory compliance, every completed transaction must be screened. A batch reprocessing job is not equivalent to real-time monitoring — the regulatory window for suspicious activity reports may be breached. This approach is only acceptable for non-regulatory workloads.

options.label: B
options.text: Reduce max.poll.records to 50 (from 500) so each poll batch takes 50 × 350ms = 17.5 seconds, well within max.poll.interval.ms. Scale back up to 8 pods (not 11) to stay within partition count. Add idempotent alert generation (deduplication key: customer_id + scenario_id + 72h window) so any duplicate processing during lag drain does not create duplicate alerts.
options.feedback: Correct on all three dimensions. (1) Reducing max.poll.records to 50 fixes the root cause: processing time per batch is now well within the 5-minute limit. (2) 8 pods for 24 partitions = 3 partitions per pod — the original assignment that was stable. (3) Idempotent alert generation (which the system should already have) handles any duplicate processing during lag drain caused by prior partial commits. The 72-hour deduplication window is the standard AML alert deduplication pattern.

options.label: C
options.text: Increase max.poll.interval.ms to 30 minutes to match the actual batch processing time. Scale to 8 pods.
options.feedback: Increasing max.poll.interval.ms to 30 minutes means a failed consumer takes 30 minutes to be detected as dead. During those 30 minutes, no other consumer picks up its partitions — 3 partitions worth of transactions go unscreened for 30 minutes. For AML, this is a 30-minute regulatory monitoring gap. The correct fix is to reduce the work per poll batch, not to extend the death-detection window.

options.label: D
options.text: Move to a separate Kafka consumer group for lag drain at high throughput, then switch back to the production group once lag is drained.
options.feedback: Two consumer groups consume the same records independently — the lag-drain group would process all 2.3M records generating its own alerts, and the production group would reprocess the same records generating duplicate alerts. Consumer group separation does not help with lag drain from the production group's committed offsets.

stages.principalRationale: The fix addresses all three dimensions: batch size (root cause of the breach), scale (operational stability), and idempotency (correctness during recovery). Financial message processing systems must be idempotent by design — lag drain and rebalances will always create redelivery scenarios.

stages.question: What leading indicator should be added to prevent this scenario from recurring during future scale-up operations?

options.label: A
options.text: Monitor consumer group lag. Alert when lag exceeds 100,000 records.
options.feedback: Consumer lag is a trailing indicator — by the time it reaches 100k, the rebalance storm is already in progress. Lag also grows for valid reasons (brief traffic spikes, deployments) that do not indicate a configuration problem. You need an indicator that surfaces the configuration risk before it manifests as a production incident.

options.label: B
options.text: Monitor the ratio of (actual processing time per poll batch) to max.poll.interval.ms. Alert when the ratio exceeds 0.6 (60% of the limit). This provides a 40% safety margin and fires before the breach, allowing preemptive reduction of max.poll.records.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the right leading indicator. If processing 50 records takes 17.5 seconds and max.poll.interval.ms is 300 seconds, the ratio is 0.058 — healthy. If record volume per batch increases or external API latency increases and ratio approaches 0.6 (180 seconds), the alert fires before the 300-second limit is breached. This gives the team time to reduce max.poll.records or investigate API latency degradation.

options.label: C
options.text: Monitor the number of rebalance events per hour. Alert when rebalances exceed 2 per hour.
options.feedback: Rebalance event monitoring is reactive — it detects the storm after it starts, not before. Normal deployments cause 1 rebalance each, so 2/hour is not an unusual threshold in a continuously deploying environment. The leading indicator must surface configuration risk, not just count rebalance events.

options.label: D
options.text: Monitor OFAC API response time P99. Alert when it exceeds 500ms, which indicates increasing processing time per record.
options.feedback: OFAC API latency monitoring is useful for SLO purposes but only captures one component of processing time. The processing time per batch depends on record count × per-record processing time. If max.poll.records increases or if records require multiple downstream calls, OFAC P99 alone will not capture the total batch time. The batch-to-limit ratio is more directly relevant.

stages.principalRationale: Leading indicators prevent incidents; trailing indicators confirm them. The poll-batch-to-interval ratio directly models the failure condition (batch duration approaching the limit) and surfaces configuration risk before it becomes a rebalance loop.

debrief.summary: max.poll.interval.ms is not about heartbeats — it measures the application's time between poll() calls. When external API calls are made per record, batch processing time scales with both record count and API latency. The fix requires reducing batch size (max.poll.records) to fit comfortably within the interval limit, combined with idempotent processing to handle the inherent redelivery of recovery scenarios.
keyTakeaways: max.poll.interval.ms controls application-level poll frequency, not network heartbeats (heartbeat.interval.ms does that)
Lag bursts at scale-up multiply poll batch sizes — worst time to have a misconfigured interval
Reduce max.poll.records to fit processing within max.poll.interval.ms with margin
All Kafka consumers in financial systems must be idempotent — rebalances and redeliveries are inevitable
Monitor poll-batch-to-interval ratio as a leading indicator, not lag as a trailing one
