scenarios.title: The GC Storm
scenarios.subtitle: JVM Full GC Pauses Breaching Payment Authorisation SLO
scenarios.context:
Payment authorisation service SLO: P99 latency < 200ms. For the past two weeks, the SLO is breached every weekday between 08:00 and 09:00 (London market open). P99 spikes to 4–8 seconds for 2–3 minutes, then self-resolves.

GC logs (enabled with -Xlog:gc*) show Full GC events lasting 3–6 seconds during the spike window. Heap is configured at 8GB. The service runs Java 21 with G1GC (default). Outside market-open hours, P99 is healthy at 85ms. The pattern is perfectly correlated with the load increase at market open.
systemConstraints: Java 21, G1GC (default configuration)
Heap: -Xms2g -Xmx8g
G1HeapRegionSize: 4MB (default for 8GB heap)
Humongous allocation threshold: > 2MB (> 50% of region size)
Market open: 08:00–09:00, 3× normal request volume
GC log: Full GC (Ergonomics) events, 3–6 second STW pauses
Normal GC: Young GC every 150ms, < 20ms pauses

stages.question: What is causing the Full GC events, and why do they only occur during market-open load?

options.label: A
options.text: G1GC's MaxGCPauseMillis target (200ms default) is too aggressive. G1GC is spending too much time trying to meet the pause target, triggering Full GC as a fallback when it cannot keep up.
options.feedback: MaxGCPauseMillis is a soft target that G1GC tries to meet by limiting collection region count per pause. When G1GC cannot keep up with allocation, it triggers a concurrent marking cycle and eventually a Full GC — but not because the pause target is too aggressive. Full GC is triggered by heap occupancy pressure, not by pause target failure. The pattern (only during peak load) points to allocation rate overwhelming concurrent collection.

options.label: B
options.text: At 3× request volume, humongous allocations (objects > 2MB, exceeding 50% of the 4MB G1 region size) are allocated directly into the old generation, bypassing young gen. G1GC cannot collect humongous objects in concurrent mixed GC cycles. When old gen fills with humongous objects, G1GC falls back to Full GC (stop-the-world). The load spike at market open pushes allocation rate past the concurrent collection capacity.
options.feedback: Correct. G1GC allocates objects larger than 50% of the region size (humongous objects) directly into one or more contiguous old-gen regions. These objects: (1) bypass the young gen allocation path, (2) are not collected in minor GCs, (3) trigger concurrent marking cycles which slow the application. Under sustained humongous allocation at peak load, old gen fills faster than concurrent collection can reclaim it, triggering a stop-the-world Full GC. The 08:00–09:00 pattern is the allocation rate threshold being crossed.

options.label: C
options.text: Kubernetes CPU throttling at market open: the pods hit their CPU limit, causing GC threads to be descheduled mid-collection, extending pause times from milliseconds to seconds.
options.feedback: CPU throttling (cgroup limits) can extend GC pause durations significantly and is a real production issue. However, the description shows Full GC events (Ergonomics) in the logs — not long Young/Mixed GCs. Ergonomics-triggered Full GC indicates G1GC chose Full GC due to heap pressure, not that it was interrupted by CPU throttling. CPU throttling would show long Young GC pause times, not Full GC.

options.label: D
options.text: The heap is growing from 2GB (-Xms2g) to 8GB (-Xmx8g) during market open. The heap expansion process itself triggers Full GC events as G1GC restructures the heap layout.
options.feedback: Heap expansion in G1GC does not trigger Full GC events. G1GC grows the heap by committing additional regions from the reserved virtual memory space — this is incremental and does not require a full heap reorganisation. Setting -Xms equal to -Xmx (avoid heap resizing) is a best practice to eliminate resize latency, but heap expansion alone does not cause multi-second Full GC events.

stages.principalRationale: Understanding G1GC's region architecture is essential for diagnosing production GC issues. Humongous allocations are a common G1GC performance trap: they bypass the carefully tuned young-gen allocation path and accumulate directly in old gen. The 50% region size threshold is the key diagnostic datum.

stages.question: What is the most effective immediate mitigation, and what investigation must accompany it?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase heap to 32GB. More old-gen space means humongous objects accumulate more slowly before triggering Full GC.
options.feedback: Increasing heap extends the interval between Full GCs but does not eliminate them. Eventually, humongous allocation rate will fill even 32GB during sustained peak load. Larger heaps also mean longer Full GC durations when they do occur (more memory to scan). This is a symptom-deferral, not a fix. The 4–6 second Full GC on 8GB would become an 8–12 second event on a 32GB heap.

options.label: B
options.text: Switch to ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC). ZGC is a concurrent collector with sub-millisecond pause times regardless of heap size. Simultaneously, enable JFR to capture allocation profiles and identify the humongous allocation sources for elimination.
options.feedback: Correct on both dimensions. ZGC eliminates stop-the-world Full GCs by performing all major collection work concurrently with the application. Sub-millisecond pauses are maintained even at 8GB+ heap sizes. JFR (Java Flight Recorder) with allocation profiling identifies exactly which call sites produce objects > 2MB — the prerequisite for the long-term fix of eliminating humongous allocations. The two actions work in parallel: ZGC stops the bleeding; JFR investigation fixes the root cause.

options.label: C
options.text: Set -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=32m. This raises the humongous threshold to 16MB, meaning most allocations are no longer classified as humongous.
options.feedback: Increasing G1HeapRegionSize is a valid G1GC-specific workaround: it raises the humongous threshold (50% of 32MB = 16MB), so objects in the 2–16MB range are no longer classified as humongous. This may resolve the issue if the humongous objects are in the 2–8MB range. However, larger regions reduce G1GC's collection granularity and can increase fragmentation. This is a reasonable G1GC-specific fix but is inferior to ZGC which eliminates the problem class entirely.

options.label: D
options.text: Schedule Kubernetes pod restarts at 07:55 every weekday to ensure a clean heap state before market open.
options.feedback: Scheduled restarts are a last resort for applications with unresolvable memory leaks. They create a brief unavailability window (pod restart + JVM warmup = 30–90 seconds of degraded service) exactly before the most critical trading period. JIT compilation warm-up effects would cause elevated latency for 2–5 minutes after restart during peak load. This solves nothing and introduces new risks.

stages.principalRationale: ZGC is the right tool for latency-sensitive financial services: its concurrent collection model gives sub-millisecond pauses at any heap size. The JFR investigation runs alongside the fix — you need both the immediate SLO protection and the root cause analysis.

stages.question: JFR allocation profiling identifies the source: the payment authorisation service builds a JSON audit record per transaction, serialises it to a byte[], and sends it to the audit service. At peak load, audit records average 2.3MB each. What is the correct long-term fix?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the audit record generation to a background thread so it does not block the authorisation response path.
options.feedback: Background threading removes the latency contribution but does not eliminate the humongous allocation. The byte[] is still created, still allocated in old gen by G1GC (or concurrently collected by ZGC). The allocation pressure problem remains, just shifted off the critical path. Keeping ZGC as the GC means this is not an immediate problem, but under extreme load the allocation rate still matters.

options.label: B
options.text: Refactor audit record serialisation to stream directly to the HTTP connection (OutputStream), eliminating the intermediate byte[] accumulation. Use a streaming JSON serialiser (Jackson's ObjectMapper.writeValue(OutputStream)) instead of ObjectMapper.writeValueAsBytes(). Verify with JFR that no allocation > 2MB occurs in the hot path.
options.feedback: Correct. The root cause is buffering the entire JSON payload into a byte[] before sending. Streaming serialisation writes directly to the HTTP output buffer in chunks — no large intermediate byte[] is ever allocated. This eliminates the humongous allocation entirely, not just for G1GC but for all future GC algorithms. JFR verification closes the loop: confirms the fix worked and the allocation profile is clean. This is defensive engineering: eliminate the problem class, not just mitigate it.

options.label: C
options.text: Compress audit records before sending. GZIP compression typically achieves 10:1 on JSON, reducing 2.3MB to 230KB — below the humongous threshold.
options.feedback: Compression reduces the final size but requires allocating the uncompressed byte[] first, compressing it into a new byte[] second. The peak allocation is still > 2MB during the compression process. The compressed output may be below the humongous threshold, but the intermediate uncompressed buffer is still humongous. Streaming compression (GZIPOutputStream wrapping the OutputStream) would address this — but the streaming serialisation approach is cleaner and avoids the CPU cost of compression.

options.label: D
options.text: Split the audit record into multiple smaller records, each < 1MB. Send 3 HTTP requests instead of 1 to avoid the humongous threshold.
options.feedback: Splitting one audit record into three sends three times the HTTP overhead, triples the number of write transactions at the audit service, and complicates audit record reconstruction. This creates correctness risk (what if 1 of 3 sends fails?) for a problem that has a clean solution at the allocation level.

stages.principalRationale: The correct fix eliminates the allocation, not just its GC classification. Streaming serialisation is a standard pattern for large payload handling in financial APIs: write to the output stream as the object graph is traversed, never materialise the whole payload in memory. This pattern also reduces memory pressure on the receiving end.

debrief.summary: G1GC humongous allocations are a common trap: objects slightly above the 50% region-size threshold bypass young-gen entirely and accumulate in old-gen. The diagnostic path is GC logs → identify Full GC trigger → JFR allocation profiling → find call sites. The fix path is ZGC as an immediate SLO protector + streaming refactor as the permanent solution.
keyTakeaways: G1GC humongous threshold: > 50% of region size (default 4MB heap → 2MB threshold)
Humongous objects bypass young gen and accumulate directly in old gen
Full GC (Ergonomics) in GC logs = heap occupancy trigger, not pause target failure
ZGC: concurrent collection, sub-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size — right choice for latency-sensitive financial services
JFR allocation profiling identifies exact call sites creating large objects
Streaming serialisation (write to OutputStream) eliminates intermediate byte[] accumulation
furtherReading: Track 09, Lesson 01 — JVM Internals: Heap Regions, GC Algorithms
Track 09, Lesson 05 — Profiling with JFR and Async-Profiler
Track 08, Lesson 02 — SLO Definition and Latency Percentiles

scenarios.title: The Phantom Trade
scenarios.subtitle: Database Isolation Failure in FX Exposure Limit Enforcement
scenarios.context:
An FX trading system enforces a £500,000 maximum exposure per trader per currency pair per day. The enforcement logic: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM fx_positions WHERE trader_id = ? AND currency_pair = ? AND trade_date = TODAY. If sum + new_trade_amount <= 500,000, allow the trade and INSERT into fx_positions.

At 10:03:17.421, two traders at different desks simultaneously submit GBP/USD trades of £450,000 each. Both read exposure = £0. Both pass the check. Both trades are inserted. Net exposure: £900,000, breaching the £500,000 limit by £400,000. The compliance team is alerted at 10:04. No application error was logged.
systemConstraints: PostgreSQL 16, READ COMMITTED isolation (default)
fx_positions table: (id, trader_id, currency_pair, amount, trade_date, created_at)
No unique constraint preventing multiple rows for the same (trader_id, currency_pair, trade_date)
2 trades submitted at exactly the same millisecond from different pods
Existing SELECT...FOR UPDATE: SELECT SUM(amount)...FOR UPDATE would acquire no lock — there are no rows yet (£0 exposure)

stages.question: What type of concurrency anomaly caused this breach, and why did SELECT...FOR UPDATE fail to prevent it?

options.label: A
options.text: Lost update: both transactions read £0 exposure and both wrote £450,000. This is the same race condition as the overdraft scenario — fix with an atomic conditional UPDATE.
options.feedback: This is not a lost update. Lost update involves two transactions reading and overwriting the same row. Here, both transactions INSERT new rows — they do not update an existing one. An atomic conditional UPDATE (WHERE SUM(amount) + new_amount <= 500000) is not syntactically valid in a single statement. The anomaly is a phantom read: a range query returns a result set that changes between two reads within the same transaction.

options.label: B
options.text: Phantom read: both transactions read the aggregate (SUM = £0) on a range of rows (WHERE trader_id = X AND currency_pair = Y AND trade_date = TODAY). At READ COMMITTED, each SELECT sees only committed data at the moment of execution — not the entire transaction's snapshot. SELECT...FOR UPDATE acquires no lock because there are no rows matching the WHERE clause at read time. When Transaction 1 commits its £450k INSERT, Transaction 2's already-completed SELECT is not re-evaluated.
options.feedback: Exactly right. This is a phantom read on an aggregate range query. SELECT...FOR UPDATE is ineffective here because it only locks existing rows. When no rows exist (£0 exposure), FOR UPDATE acquires zero locks. Transaction 2 reads £0 (correct at that instant), passes the check, and proceeds to insert — unaware that Transaction 1 is concurrently doing the same. The fix requires an isolation level that detects this write-write conflict: SERIALIZABLE.

options.label: C
options.text: Dirty read: Transaction 2 read Transaction 1's uncommitted £450,000 insert, but due to a database bug, the read returned £0 instead of the correct pending value.
options.feedback: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads by definition — it only returns committed data. There is no database bug here. Transaction 2 correctly returned £0 because Transaction 1 had not yet committed. The problem is that the check logic requires knowing about concurrent in-flight transactions, which READ COMMITTED cannot provide.

options.label: D
options.text: Network partition between the two application pods caused both to miss each other's in-progress transactions.
options.feedback: Application pods do not communicate with each other about in-progress transactions — the database is the coordination point. A network partition between pods would not affect their independent connections to the same PostgreSQL instance. Both transactions execute correctly against the database; the problem is the database isolation level not preventing their concurrent execution.

stages.principalRationale: Phantom reads on aggregate queries are a subtle and dangerous isolation anomaly. SELECT...FOR UPDATE only locks existing rows — it cannot lock the absence of rows (the range). This is why SERIALIZABLE was invented: it detects that two transactions accessed overlapping ranges and that the concurrent inserts make at least one transaction's read result incorrect.

stages.question: What is the correct isolation level fix, and what is the trade-off you must manage in production?

options.label: A
options.text: Use REPEATABLE READ isolation. This prevents phantom reads by taking a snapshot at transaction start.
options.feedback: PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ does prevent some phantoms via MVCC snapshot isolation, but it does not prevent write-write conflicts in this exact scenario. Two concurrent transactions under REPEATABLE READ can both read a consistent snapshot (£0), both pass the check, and both insert — PostgreSQL does not detect the aggregate range conflict under REPEATABLE READ. Only SERIALIZABLE detects this via predicate locking.

options.label: B
options.text: Use SERIALIZABLE isolation with retry logic: PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE uses SSI (Serialisable Snapshot Isolation) to detect read-write conflicts. When two transactions access overlapping ranges and both proceed to write, one is aborted with serialisation error (SQLSTATE 40001). The application must catch 40001 and retry. At low concurrency, retries are rare; at high concurrency, retry rate must be monitored.
options.feedback: Correct. PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE + SSI detects the predicate conflict (overlapping range reads + concurrent inserts) and aborts the conflicting transaction with error code 40001. The application retries the aborted transaction, which now reads £450,000 existing exposure, fails the £500,000 check, and correctly declines the trade. The trade-off: serialisation failures add latency for aborted transactions and require robust retry logic. At the trade submission frequency of an FX desk, the retry rate is acceptable.

options.label: C
options.text: Use an advisory lock keyed on (trader_id, currency_pair, date) to serialise concurrent exposure checks for the same trader.
options.feedback: Advisory locks (pg_advisory_xact_lock) are a valid approach: they serialise access at the application level for a given lock key. This prevents concurrent transactions from simultaneously checking and modifying the same trader's exposure. The downside versus SERIALIZABLE: advisory locks must be explicitly acquired and released, and their scope is the entire (trader_id, currency_pair, date) combination — meaning two traders checking different currency pairs would not block each other (correct) but two traders with the same key would queue (acceptable). This works but requires more application code than SERIALIZABLE.

options.label: D
options.text: Add a unique constraint on (trader_id, currency_pair, trade_date) so only one row per trader per day can exist. Use UPDATE ... SET amount = amount + ? to atomically accumulate the exposure.
options.feedback: This is a viable alternative architecture: accumulate exposure in a single row using an atomic UPDATE instead of INSERT per trade. This turns the phantom read into an atomic update problem (which is well-solved). However, it requires changing the data model from an append-only trade log to a mutable running total — losing the per-trade audit trail. Financial systems typically require the per-trade record for regulatory reporting. The model change is a larger refactor than fixing the isolation level.

stages.principalRationale: SERIALIZABLE is the correct tool when business correctness requires that concurrent aggregate reads and conditional inserts are mutually exclusive. The retry mechanism is not optional — it is the application's responsibility to handle SQLSTATE 40001 gracefully.

stages.question: After deploying SERIALIZABLE isolation, you observe that 3% of trade submissions require a retry. The desk head asks whether the retried trades could ever breach the limit. What is your answer?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — retried transactions read a fresh snapshot of exposure that may not reflect all in-flight transactions at the time of retry.
options.feedback: SERIALIZABLE transactions read the latest committed data at retry time. Under SERIALIZABLE isolation, 'in-flight' transactions either committed or were aborted before the retry reads. There is no window where the retry sees stale data — it sees all committed exposure including the trade that caused the original transaction to abort.

options.label: B
options.text: No. A retried transaction begins a new SERIALIZABLE transaction. It reads the current committed exposure (including the trade that caused the abort). If the exposure plus the new trade exceeds £500,000, the check correctly fails and the trade is declined. SERIALIZABLE ensures the retry operates on a consistent view that includes all committed transactions.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the guarantee that makes SERIALIZABLE valuable for financial systems. The retried transaction cannot see less exposure than actually committed. The serialisation abort was precisely to prevent the double-commit — on retry, the full £450,000 is visible, the check fails (£450k + £450k = £900k > £500k limit), and the trade is correctly declined. The system behaves as if the trades were processed serially.

options.label: C
options.text: Only if the retry happens within 100ms of the original abort, before the conflicting transaction commits.
options.feedback: SERIALIZABLE transactions are aborted precisely because the conflicting transaction has already committed (or is guaranteed to commit). A SERIALIZABLE abort means: 'your transaction is inconsistent with another committed transaction.' By the time the abort is returned to the application, the conflicting transaction has committed. The retry always sees committed exposure.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — under SSI, PostgreSQL occasionally aborts transactions speculatively. A retried transaction may operate on data that is actually consistent, re-testing a constraint that was not actually violated.
options.feedback: SSI false aborts (conservative aborts where no actual anomaly occurred) are possible in theory but are extremely rare in practice for this access pattern. Even when they occur, the retry sees consistent data and re-evaluates the exposure check correctly — it may unnecessarily abort a valid trade but it cannot approve a trade that breaches the limit. False aborts are a performance concern, not a correctness concern.

stages.principalRationale: The desk head's question is about financial correctness, not performance. Under SERIALIZABLE, retried transactions always operate on the full committed state — they cannot approve a limit-breaching trade. This guarantee is the entire point of SERIALIZABLE isolation for financial constraint enforcement.

debrief.summary: Phantom reads on aggregate range queries are the isolation anomaly that READ COMMITTED and even REPEATABLE READ cannot prevent. SERIALIZABLE isolation with PostgreSQL's SSI detects predicate conflicts and aborts one of the conflicting transactions. The application must handle SQLSTATE 40001 with retry logic. The retry is always safe: it sees the full committed exposure and cannot approve a breaching trade.
keyTakeaways: SELECT...FOR UPDATE only locks existing rows — it cannot prevent phantom inserts into the range
READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ do not prevent aggregate range phantoms
SERIALIZABLE + SSI detects predicate conflicts and aborts with SQLSTATE 40001
Applications must handle 40001 with retry logic — this is part of the contract with SERIALIZABLE
Retried transactions always see full committed state — correctness is preserved
furtherReading: Track 10, Lesson 01 — ACID Properties and Transaction Isolation
Track 10, Lesson 04 — Isolation Levels: Anomalies and Trade-offs
Track 03, Lesson 06 — Spring Transactions and Database Locking

scenarios.title: The Duplicate Charge
scenarios.subtitle: Race Condition in Idempotency Key Check Causes Double Charge
scenarios.context:
A mobile banking app sends POST /payments with an Idempotency-Key UUID header on every request. The server checks for an existing key, processes the payment if new, and returns the cached result if duplicate. Standard pattern.

At 14:22, a customer submits a £1,200 rent payment. The request times out after 28 seconds (mobile app timeout). The app displays an error. The customer taps 'Pay' again, which sends the same Idempotency-Key (the app retains the UUID for retries). Both requests succeed. The customer is charged £2,400.

The server logs show both requests arrived within 180ms of each other (network retry) with identical Idempotency-Key values. No duplicate-key error was logged.
systemConstraints: Idempotency check: SELECT id FROM idempotency_keys WHERE key = ?
If not found: INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, result), process payment, UPDATE idempotency_keys SET result = ?
PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED
No UNIQUE constraint on idempotency_keys.key
Both requests hit different application pods behind a load balancer
Mobile app timeout: 28 seconds (server processed in 25 seconds)

stages.question: Both requests carried identical Idempotency-Key values. Why did the idempotency check fail to prevent the duplicate payment?

options.label: A
options.text: The mobile app sent different Idempotency-Key values despite displaying the same UUID to the developer. A client-side UUID generation bug produced two different keys.
options.feedback: The problem statement specifies identical keys. If keys were different, the idempotency check would not apply — this would be two independent payments, which is a different problem. Assuming server-side root causes when client-side bugs are unconfirmed is a diagnostic shortcut. The server logs should confirm identical keys — and in this case they do.

options.label: B
options.text: Check-then-act race condition: both requests hit different pods simultaneously. Pod A reads: 'key not found'. Pod B reads: 'key not found'. Both proceed to process the payment. Pod A inserts the key and commits. Pod B inserts a duplicate key and commits (no UNIQUE constraint to prevent it). The idempotency check is a classic read-then-write without atomicity guarantee.
options.feedback: Exactly right. The idempotency pattern is only correct if the 'check and claim' operation is atomic. With two pods executing concurrently under READ COMMITTED, both reads legitimately return 'key not found' before either write commits. Without a UNIQUE constraint enforcing at the database level that only one insert succeeds, both inserts proceed. The fix must make the check-and-claim atomic at the database level.

options.label: C
options.text: Redis cache for idempotency keys was down. The fallback path skipped the idempotency check and processed all payments.
options.feedback: If the architecture includes Redis for idempotency caching and Redis was down, the fallback should fail closed (reject requests) or fall back to the database, not skip the check entirely. However, the problem description shows a database-only implementation — the race condition is at the database level regardless of Redis availability.

options.label: D
options.text: The 28-second processing time caused the idempotency key to expire before the second request arrived. Idempotency keys have a 10-second TTL.
options.feedback: The problem description does not mention a TTL. More importantly, the second request arrived 180ms after the first — well within any reasonable TTL. The expiry theory would require a TTL shorter than 180ms, which would make the idempotency system useless. The race condition during the initial check is the correct diagnosis.

stages.principalRationale: Idempotency systems fail in exactly the same way as balance checks without atomic operations: the check-then-act pattern has a race window. The database UNIQUE constraint closes this window at the storage layer — it is the last line of defence that cannot be bypassed by application-level races.

stages.question: What is the correct implementation to make idempotency checks race-condition-proof?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a Redis distributed lock keyed on the Idempotency-Key. First request acquires the lock (10s expiry), processes the payment, releases the lock. Second request tries to acquire the lock, fails, waits, then checks if the result is available.
options.feedback: Redis distributed locks can work but introduce two failure modes: (1) if the lock holder pod crashes after payment processing but before releasing the lock, the second request waits 10 seconds then reprocesses, defeating idempotency; (2) if Redis is unavailable, the entire idempotency system fails. This adds an external dependency to the critical payment path. The database UNIQUE constraint approach is simpler and more reliable.

options.label: B
options.text: Add UNIQUE constraint on idempotency_keys(key). Use INSERT...ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (or ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE). The first insert wins; all subsequent inserts for the same key are silently ignored. After insert, check if the returned row was inserted by this request or a prior one. Return the prior result if found.
options.feedback: Correct. The UNIQUE constraint makes the database the arbiter: exactly one insert succeeds per key, enforced by the database engine's index uniqueness check, which is atomic even under concurrent transactions. INSERT...ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING returns 0 rows inserted for duplicates; the application checks the rowcount to determine if this is the first request (process payment) or a duplicate (return cached result). No application-level lock needed. No external dependency. Race-condition-proof.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a SERIALIZABLE transaction for the idempotency check. The SELECT and INSERT are within the same SERIALIZABLE transaction, ensuring no concurrent transaction can insert the same key simultaneously.
options.feedback: SERIALIZABLE helps with range phantoms but not with this specific pattern. Two concurrent SERIALIZABLE transactions can both read 'key not found' and both attempt to insert the same key. Without a UNIQUE constraint, both inserts succeed. Without the UNIQUE constraint to generate a conflict, SERIALIZABLE does not detect a predicate conflict on a point lookup (single key). The UNIQUE constraint alone (at READ COMMITTED) is sufficient and simpler.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the payment's amount + account ID + timestamp (truncated to 1 second) as a natural idempotency key instead of a UUID. Duplicate payments within 1 second will have identical natural keys.
options.feedback: Natural keys based on amount + account + timestamp are not idempotent: a customer legitimately paying the same amount to the same account within 1 second would be incorrectly deduplicated. The UUID idempotency key generated by the mobile app is the correct approach — it uniquely identifies a specific payment attempt. The problem is the race condition in the check implementation, not the key design.

stages.principalRationale: The database UNIQUE constraint is the simplest, most reliable idempotency enforcement mechanism. It requires no external dependencies, adds no latency beyond the index check, and is race-condition-proof by design. INSERT...ON CONFLICT is the atomic check-and-claim that the application-level read-then-write pattern cannot provide.

stages.question: The fix is deployed. What idempotency key expiry policy is correct for a retail payment API?

options.label: A
options.text: Idempotency keys should never expire — retain them indefinitely to ensure duplicate requests can always be detected.
options.feedback: Indefinite retention creates unbounded storage growth and the idempotency_keys table becomes the largest table in the database over time. More importantly, a key from 2 years ago is not a 'duplicate payment' — it is a customer making the same payment again (e.g., monthly rent). Indefinite retention would prevent legitimate repeat payments with the same UUID if the mobile app reuses old keys.

options.label: B
options.text: Retain idempotency keys for 24 hours. After expiry, a request with the same key is treated as a new payment. Document this as an API contract: clients must use a fresh UUID for payments submitted more than 24 hours after a previous attempt.
options.feedback: Correct. 24 hours covers all realistic retry scenarios: network timeouts, app crashes, mobile background refresh delays. After 24 hours, the original payment either completed (customer already has the money) or failed (safe to retry with a new key). The 24-hour window must be documented explicitly in the API contract so client developers understand the retry semantics. PSD2 and similar regulations require payment idempotency windows of at least the settlement day.

options.label: C
options.text: Expire idempotency keys after 60 seconds to minimise storage. Retries must occur within 60 seconds of the original request.
options.feedback: 60-second expiry is insufficient for real-world retry scenarios. Mobile apps may be backgrounded for minutes, networks may be intermittent, and customers may not retry immediately. A 60-second window means the idempotency protection disappears before most retry attempts occur — the system would behave as if no idempotency keys exist for the common case.

options.label: D
options.text: Expire idempotency keys after 7 days, matching the standard bank statement reconciliation period.
options.feedback: 7 days provides strong duplicate protection but creates a user experience problem: a customer who gets an error on a payment cannot retry with a fresh payment for 7 days using the same amount to the same recipient without changing their UUID. 24 hours is the standard adopted by Stripe, Plaid, and most major payment APIs — it balances duplicate protection against legitimate retry freedom.

stages.principalRationale: Idempotency key expiry policy is an API contract decision with business and regulatory implications. 24 hours covers all realistic retry scenarios while allowing legitimate repeat payments. Document it explicitly — clients need to understand the boundary between 'duplicate' and 'new payment'.

debrief.summary: The idempotency pattern fails at the same point as all check-then-act patterns: the race window between reading 'not found' and inserting the claim. The UNIQUE constraint closes this window at the database level — the first insert wins, subsequent inserts return ON CONFLICT. Combined with a well-defined expiry policy, this provides production-grade idempotency for payment APIs.
keyTakeaways: Idempotency check-then-act has a race window identical to the overdraft lost update problem
UNIQUE constraint + INSERT...ON CONFLICT is the atomic, race-condition-proof implementation
No external lock dependencies (Redis, Zookeeper) needed for database-backed idempotency
24-hour key expiry is the industry standard for retail payment APIs
Mobile apps must retain the UUID for the duration of the retry window, not generate a new one on each retry

scenarios.title: The Database Migration Deadline
scenarios.subtitle: Zero-Downtime Column Addition on an 800 Million Row Table
scenarios.context:
The compliance team requires a new `risk_score NUMERIC(5,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00` column on the `payment_transactions` table. The table has 800 million rows and receives 20,000 inserts per second.

The DBA estimates the naive ALTER TABLE will take 6 hours (full table rewrite, exclusive lock held throughout). Business has approved a Saturday maintenance window of 15 minutes. Product says any longer window is unacceptable due to PSD2 real-time payment requirements.

Engineering must deliver the column addition before next Wednesday's regulatory audit.
systemConstraints: payment_transactions: 800M rows, 20,000 inserts/second
PostgreSQL 16, primary + 2 read replicas
Replication lag budget: < 5 seconds
Current table size: ~400GB
Maintenance window: Saturday 02:00–02:15 (15 minutes)
Deployment pipeline: Flyway migrations run on application startup
Application pods: 12, rolling deployment

stages.question: Why does `ALTER TABLE payment_transactions ADD COLUMN risk_score NUMERIC(5,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00` take 6 hours, and what lock does it hold?

options.label: A
options.text: PostgreSQL must verify the NOT NULL constraint by scanning all 800M rows. The constraint check takes approximately 400 seconds at 2M rows/second, holding a ShareLock that allows reads but blocks writes.
options.feedback: Partially correct on the scan component, but misidentifies the lock type and operation. PostgreSQL requires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock (the strongest lock — blocks all reads and writes) for most ALTER TABLE operations. For a NOT NULL column with a DEFAULT, PostgreSQL must rewrite every row to include the new column value in the tuple — this is not just a constraint scan.

options.label: B
options.text: Adding a NOT NULL column with a constant DEFAULT requires PostgreSQL to rewrite every row in the table to include the new column value. 800M rows × ~50 bytes per row rewrite = ~40GB written. At typical I/O rates (100MB/s write), this takes 400 seconds minimum, plus index rebuilds and checkpoint overhead. An ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock is held for the entire duration — blocking all reads and writes.
options.feedback: Correct. PostgreSQL pre-13 always rewrote the table for NOT NULL + DEFAULT. PostgreSQL 11+ added an optimisation: for constant DEFAULT values (not volatile functions), the default is stored in catalog metadata and rows are rewritten lazily. However, the NOT NULL constraint still requires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the validation scan. On an 800M row table with active write load, even the 'fast path' can take many minutes due to vacuum, checkpoint, and replication pressure. The 6-hour estimate reflects a worst-case scenario including index rebuilds.

options.label: C
options.text: The operation requires stopping replication to all read replicas while the table is being modified, then resyncing the replicas from scratch after the modification completes.
options.feedback: PostgreSQL ALTER TABLE is replicated via WAL streaming — replicas apply the same ALTER TABLE DDL from the WAL stream. There is no need to stop or resync replicas. Replication lag will increase significantly during the operation (all those row rewrites generate enormous WAL), but replicas continue operating throughout.

options.label: D
options.text: PostgreSQL must rebuild all existing indexes on the table to incorporate the new column into the index metadata, even if the new column is not indexed.
options.feedback: Existing indexes do not need to be rebuilt when adding a new column that is not part of those indexes. Index entries reference row versions (ctid), not column positions directly. Adding an unindexed column does not invalidate existing index entries.

stages.principalRationale: Understanding what PostgreSQL actually does during DDL operations is essential for production database management. ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock + full table rewrite on 800M rows is a production-stopping event. Knowing the PostgreSQL version's optimisations (constant default metadata storage) helps scope the actual work, but the lock duration remains the primary constraint.

stages.question: What is the correct zero-downtime migration strategy for this column addition?

options.label: A
options.text: Use pg_repack to perform an online table rebuild: creates a new table with the extra column, copies rows in background, swaps old table with new atomically. The swap requires a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock (< 1 second).
options.feedback: pg_repack is a valid tool for some online table restructuring scenarios, but it requires disk space equal to the table size (400GB free), runs a full table copy (hours), and the final swap lock — while brief — must wait for all current transactions to finish. On a 20,000 TPS table, long-running transactions can block the swap for minutes. It is also an external tool requiring careful installation and version matching. The expand-contract pattern is simpler and fully supported by standard PostgreSQL.

options.label: B
options.text: Expand-contract pattern across 3 deployments: (1) Add column as NULLABLE (no default, no NOT NULL) — PostgreSQL does this in milliseconds with no row rewrite; (2) Backfill in batches of 10,000 rows using UPDATE with rate limiting; (3) Add NOT NULL constraint using ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID, then separately VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in background (ShareUpdateExclusiveLock, does not block reads/writes); (4) Update application code to write risk_score; (5) Drop the nullable nature if needed.
options.feedback: Correct. The expand-contract pattern is the industry-standard zero-downtime migration approach. Each step is independently safe: (1) Nullable column addition in milliseconds — no row rewrite in PostgreSQL 11+; (2) Batched backfill with rate limiting avoids I/O saturation; (3) NOT VALID skips existing row validation, allowing the constraint to apply to new rows immediately; VALIDATE CONSTRAINT uses a non-blocking lock that runs concurrently with queries. The entire migration happens live with zero downtime and no maintenance window needed.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a blue-green deployment: provision a new database, run the full ALTER TABLE on the new database, synchronise data via logical replication, then switch the application connection string to the new database.
options.feedback: Blue-green database deployments are expensive and complex: provisioning a 400GB replica, running ALTER TABLE on it (still hours), synchronising via logical replication (which cannot replicate DDL automatically — needs careful setup), and switching connection strings without dropped transactions is an orchestration challenge. This is appropriate for database engine upgrades but is overkill for adding a single column.

options.label: D
options.text: Split the 15-minute maintenance window across 3 Saturdays: add the column (5 min), backfill (5 min), add constraint (5 min). The table is unavailable for 5 minutes each Saturday.
options.feedback: Even 5 minutes of unavailability violates PSD2 real-time payment requirements. Additionally, 5 minutes is insufficient to backfill 800M rows — at 20,000 updates/second (maximum safe rate), you can update 6M rows in 5 minutes, leaving 794M rows unbackfilled. The expand-contract pattern eliminates the need for any maintenance window.

stages.principalRationale: The expand-contract (also called the parallel-change) pattern is essential knowledge for principal engineers. It decomposes a blocking DDL operation into a sequence of non-blocking steps. NOT VALID + VALIDATE CONSTRAINT is the PostgreSQL mechanism that allows constraint enforcement to be decoupled from constraint validation — the key technique enabling online migrations.

stages.question: During the backfill phase (step 2), what is the correct batching strategy to avoid production impact?

options.label: A
options.text: Run a single UPDATE payment_transactions SET risk_score = 0.00 WHERE risk_score IS NULL. PostgreSQL will use MVCC to avoid blocking reads.
options.feedback: A single UPDATE on 800M rows would hold a lock on each row as it is processed. While MVCC allows concurrent reads of old row versions, the UPDATE itself generates 800M row rewrites, saturates I/O, generates enormous WAL (triggering replication lag > 5 second budget), and runs for hours. The absence of a table-level lock does not make this safe — the I/O impact would severely degrade the production system.

options.label: B
options.text: Batch update in chunks of 1,000–10,000 rows using the row's primary key range: UPDATE ... WHERE id BETWEEN :start AND :end AND risk_score IS NULL. Sleep 10ms between batches. Monitor replication lag and I/O utilisation; pause the job if lag exceeds 3 seconds or disk utilisation exceeds 70%.
options.feedback: Correct. Small-batch updates with rate limiting give production traffic the I/O headroom to continue processing. The sleep interval is adjustable — pause more aggressively during peak hours, run faster during off-peak. Monitoring replication lag provides direct feedback: if lag increases, reduce batch rate. The 3-second lag threshold provides a 2-second buffer before the 5-second budget is breached. This backfill approach is used by all major SQL migration tools (gh-ost, Flyway online migrations, pt-online-schema-change).

options.label: C
options.text: Run the backfill job on a read replica to avoid impacting the primary. When complete, promote the replica as the new primary.
options.feedback: Read replicas apply changes from the primary via WAL streaming — they cannot accept writes directly (unless promoted). Running writes on a read replica would require promoting it, which makes it the new primary and leaves the old primary as a detached standalone instance. This is not a backfill strategy — it is a failover, and would be catastrophic for data integrity.

options.label: D
options.text: Parallelise the backfill with 8 worker threads, each processing a different primary key range. This completes the backfill 8× faster without I/O impact since each thread's updates are independent.
options.feedback: Parallelising with 8 workers multiplies I/O pressure 8×. The I/O impact is not independent per thread — all threads compete for the same disk bandwidth. 8 parallel workers would saturate I/O much faster than a single-threaded batcher and would likely push replication lag well past the 5-second budget. Rate-limiting a single thread and monitoring lag is the correct approach; parallelism can be cautiously increased only if I/O headroom exists.

stages.principalRationale: Backfill operations on live tables must be treated as production workloads, not maintenance tasks. The rate-limiting strategy (small batches + sleep + lag monitoring) is the standard approach used by all production database migration tools. The monitoring feedback loop is essential: the backfill rate must adapt to production load.

debrief.summary: Zero-downtime schema migrations require decomposing blocking DDL into non-blocking steps. The expand-contract pattern — add nullable, backfill in rate-limited batches, add NOT VALID constraint, validate concurrently — is the standard technique. Never run a table-rewriting ALTER TABLE on a live production table with hundreds of millions of rows.
keyTakeaways: ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN NOT NULL DEFAULT requires ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and potentially full table rewrite
Nullable column addition in PostgreSQL 11+ is near-instantaneous — no row rewrite for constant defaults
NOT VALID skips existing row validation; VALIDATE CONSTRAINT runs with a non-blocking ShareUpdateExclusiveLock
Backfill in small batches (1k-10k rows) with sleep intervals and replication lag monitoring
Flyway/Liquibase migrations in CI must include the expand-contract sequence, not raw ALTER TABLE
furtherReading: Track 10, Lesson 09 — Online Schema Migrations
Track 10, Lesson 05 — PostgreSQL Locking and MVCC
Track 12, Lesson 06 — Kubernetes Rolling Deployments and Database Compatibility

scenarios.title: The Outbox Failure
scenarios.subtitle: Dual-Write Failure Leaves £3.2M in Payments Unprocessed
scenarios.context:
Payment service flow: (1) validate payment, (2) commit to PostgreSQL (`payment_transactions` table), (3) publish `payment.authorised` event to Kafka for downstream settlement processing.

After a Friday deployment, monitoring shows 847 payments committed to PostgreSQL but no corresponding Kafka events. Settlement service lag counter reads 0 — it has not consumed any new events in 4 hours. £3.2M in authorised payments have not been submitted for settlement.

The Kafka broker logs show no errors. The payment service logs show Kafka producer errors for a 12-minute window (14:03–14:15) on Friday — during which a broker restarted — then healthy publishing resumed. The 847 unprocessed payments all fall within that 12-minute window.
systemConstraints: Payment service: Spring Boot, @Transactional commit then kafkaTemplate.send()
KafkaTemplate: fire-and-forget (no producer callback checked for 14:03-14:15 window)
Kafka cluster: 3 brokers, replication factor 3, acks=all
Settlement service: Kafka consumer, offset management: auto-commit
No outbox table in current schema
Payments in DB: committed, status=AUTHORISED
Kafka events: missing for the 12-minute window

stages.question: What is the fundamental architectural problem that caused the 847 missing events?

options.label: A
options.text: The Kafka broker restart caused the payment service's producer to reconnect. During reconnection, the in-flight send() calls were silently dropped.
options.feedback: Broker restarts do cause producer reconnection and can cause send failures. However, with acks=all, the producer should receive an error on failed sends, allowing the application to retry or handle the error. The deeper issue is that even if the error was surfaced, the application had no mechanism to durably retry — the payment was already committed to the database and there was no record that the Kafka event was not published.

options.label: B
options.text: The dual-write problem: the PostgreSQL commit and the Kafka publish are two independent operations with no atomicity guarantee. The commit succeeded; the Kafka publish failed (broker restart). These two writes cannot be wrapped in a distributed transaction. Without the Transactional Outbox pattern, there is no way to guarantee that a committed payment always produces a Kafka event.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the dual-write problem: two distributed systems (database + message broker) cannot participate in a single atomic transaction without a coordinator. Any pattern that does 'commit DB, then publish Kafka' has a failure window between the two operations. The Transactional Outbox eliminates this by converting the dual-write into a single-write (DB only) followed by a reliable relay process.

options.label: C
options.text: The settlement service's Kafka auto-commit advanced past the missing events. The events were published but marked as consumed before settlement processing completed.
options.feedback: If events were published, the settlement service would have consumed them. The problem is that the events were never published — Kafka consumer auto-commit is irrelevant when the producer side failed. Settlement service lag = 0 confirms it has not consumed any new events, not that it consumed and lost them.

options.label: D
options.text: The Kafka topic's retention period expired for the 14:03-14:15 events before the settlement service could consume them.
options.feedback: Kafka default retention is 7 days or 1 week. 4 hours is nowhere near a typical retention boundary. More fundamentally, the payment service logs show producer errors — the events were never written to Kafka, not written and later expired.

stages.principalRationale: The dual-write problem is fundamental: any architecture that writes to two independent systems sequentially has an atomicity gap. This is not a bug in the implementation — it is an architectural property of the pattern. The only solutions are: (1) accept the gap and add compensating monitoring, or (2) redesign to eliminate the dual write with the Transactional Outbox pattern.

stages.question: What is the correct architectural fix to prevent this recurrence?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Kafka's exactly-once semantics (enable.idempotence=true + transactional.id). Wrap the PostgreSQL commit and Kafka publish in a Kafka transaction. If the Kafka transaction fails, the PostgreSQL transaction is rolled back via two-phase commit.
options.feedback: Kafka's transactional API provides exactly-once semantics within Kafka (read-process-write atomicity between Kafka topics). It does not provide distributed transactions between Kafka and PostgreSQL — there is no two-phase commit coordination between them. Rolling back a PostgreSQL commit based on a Kafka failure is not possible without XA transactions, which are not supported by standard Kafka producers.

options.label: B
options.text: Transactional Outbox: within the same PostgreSQL transaction as the payment insert, also insert a row into an outbox table (payment_id, event_type, payload, published=false). A separate relay process (Debezium CDC reading the outbox table, or a polling worker) reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka. Mark outbox rows as published after successful Kafka acknowledgement. The relay ensures at-least-once Kafka delivery; idempotent consumers handle duplicates.
options.feedback: Correct. The Transactional Outbox eliminates the dual write: the payment and the outbox record are committed atomically in a single PostgreSQL transaction. If the transaction commits, the outbox record exists. If Kafka is down, the relay retries until it succeeds — the outbox row guarantees the event will eventually be published. The relay is decoupled from the payment service: Kafka downtime does not cause payment failures, only event delay. This is the standard pattern for event-driven financial systems.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a producer callback to kafkaTemplate.send(): on failure, log the error and add the payment ID to a Redis retry queue. A background job retries the Kafka publish from the retry queue.
options.feedback: This is better than fire-and-forget but is a leaky abstraction: Redis becomes a critical dependency in the payment flow, and the Redis write itself can fail (dual-write problem recurse). The retry queue is also not durable across pod restarts unless Redis is configured with persistence. The Transactional Outbox in PostgreSQL is simpler and more reliable — the database you already trust for payment durability also stores the event obligation.

options.label: D
options.text: Move to a choreography-based Saga: payment service does not publish to Kafka directly. Instead, settlement service polls the payment_transactions table for new AUTHORISED rows every 30 seconds.
options.feedback: Polling is a valid pattern but introduces 30-second settlement latency. At 20,000 TPS, the settlement service would be processing events 10 minutes old during catch-up after a brief outage. Event-driven architectures exist precisely to avoid polling latency. The Transactional Outbox maintains the event-driven architecture while solving the durability problem.

stages.principalRationale: The Transactional Outbox converts an unreliable dual-write into a reliable single-write (DB) + relay. The relay can fail and retry indefinitely because the outbox row is durable — the event obligation survives pod restarts, Kafka downtime, and network partitions.

stages.question: After deploying the Transactional Outbox, what metric provides the best ongoing assurance that events are being relayed to Kafka promptly?

options.label: A
options.text: Monitor Kafka consumer lag on the settlement topic. Alert if lag exceeds 10,000 events.
options.feedback: Settlement consumer lag measures whether the settlement service is keeping up with published events — not whether the outbox relay is publishing them. If the relay stops publishing, the settlement consumer lag stays at 0 (no new events to consume), giving a false sense of health. You need a metric that directly monitors the outbox relay's publishing latency.

options.label: B
options.text: Monitor the outbox table: count of rows with published=false AND created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '60 seconds'. Alert when count > 0. Any unpublished outbox record older than 60 seconds indicates relay failure.
options.feedback: Correct. This directly monitors the outbox relay's health: if any event obligation is older than 60 seconds and still unpublished, the relay is failing or stuck. 60 seconds is the SLO for event propagation latency — tighten or loosen based on settlement latency requirements. This metric is independent of Kafka consumer lag (which only measures consumption, not production) and directly answers: 'is every committed payment event being relayed to Kafka within SLO?'

options.label: C
options.text: Monitor the relay process's JVM memory and CPU. If resource consumption is healthy, the relay is working correctly.
options.feedback: Process health (JVM memory/CPU) measures whether the relay is running, not whether it is successfully publishing events. A relay that runs but fails every Kafka send due to a serialisation bug would appear healthy by JVM metrics while publishing zero events. Monitor the outbox table directly — it is the source of truth for unpublished event obligations.

options.label: D
options.text: Monitor the settlement service's processed payment count per minute. If the rate drops below 15,000/minute, alert.
options.feedback: Settlement throughput monitoring is a business-level SLO metric. It detects degradation but is a downstream trailing indicator — by the time the settlement rate drops, the outbox backlog may already be significant. The outbox age metric provides a leading indicator that fires before settlement throughput is impacted.

stages.principalRationale: Monitor the outbox directly — it is the contract between the database and Kafka. Any unpublished obligation older than the SLO threshold is a relay failure. This metric is precise, directly actionable (shows exactly which payments are affected), and independent of downstream consumer behaviour.

debrief.summary: The dual-write problem is an architectural constant: writing to two independent systems sequentially always has an atomicity gap. The Transactional Outbox pattern solves this by converting the dual write into a single atomic write (DB) plus a reliable relay. The outbox table is the durable contract — the event will be published eventually, regardless of transient Kafka or relay failures.
keyTakeaways: Dual-write: DB commit then Kafka publish has an atomicity gap — Kafka publish can fail silently
Transactional Outbox: payment + outbox record committed atomically in one DB transaction
Relay (Debezium CDC or polling loop) publishes outbox records to Kafka with at-least-once delivery
Idempotent Kafka consumers handle the rare duplicate that relay retries produce
Monitor outbox age (unpublished rows > 60s), not Kafka consumer lag, for relay health

scenarios.title: The Memory Leak
scenarios.subtitle: JVM OOM from Unbounded Cache Accumulating PDF Byte Arrays
scenarios.context:
Payment gateway pods restart every 4–6 hours with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. This started exactly 3 weeks ago after releasing a new PDF statement generation feature. Normal pod memory usage: 400MB. Pods restart at ~3.8GB heap used.

The team increased -Xmx from 2GB to 4GB two weeks ago, which extended pod lifetime from 2 hours to 4-6 hours without fixing the underlying issue. Kubernetes liveness probes restart pods on OOM, so availability is maintained (new pod starts in ~45 seconds). However, restarts coincide with peak transaction hours, causing elevated latency.
systemConstraints: Java 21, Spring Boot, -Xmx4g, G1GC
12 pods behind Kubernetes load balancer
PDF statement feature: generates account statements on demand via REST API GET /statements/{accountId}
JFR continuous recording enabled (default settings)
Heap dump on OOM: enabled (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError)
OOM heap dump size: 3.8GB — available in PersistentVolume
Memory growth: linear, ~600MB/hour at normal load

stages.question: Before analysing the heap dump, what is the most likely root cause based on the symptoms alone?

options.label: A
options.text: The PDF generation library has a native memory leak. It allocates off-heap memory via JNI that the JVM garbage collector cannot reclaim.
options.feedback: Off-heap (native) memory leaks would manifest as pod-level memory exhaustion (Kubernetes OOMKill at the cgroup limit) without an OutOfMemoryError in JVM heap. The symptoms describe an OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space — this is an on-heap issue. If the GC cannot reclaim heap despite running, something is holding strong references to heap-allocated objects. Native memory leaks are a separate issue with different symptoms.

options.label: B
options.text: The PDF feature populates a cache (likely a static Map or Spring @Cacheable bean) with the generated PDF byte[] data, keyed by accountId. The cache has no eviction policy or size limit. Every statement request adds ~2MB of byte[] to the cache. After 3 weeks of usage, the cache has grown to consume all available heap. GC cannot collect the byte[] because the cache holds strong references.
options.feedback: Correct. The pattern — linear memory growth starting exactly when a caching feature was released, dominated by byte[] in the heap dump — is the signature of an unbounded cache accumulating large objects. PDF byte arrays (~2MB each) with no eviction mean every unique account statement request adds 2MB permanently. After 3 weeks, tens of thousands of cached PDFs fill the heap. GC sees them as live objects (cache holds strong references) and cannot collect them.

options.label: C
options.text: HTTP session objects from PDF download requests are accumulating in memory. Each PDF download session is not being invalidated, holding a reference to the byte[] response body.
options.feedback: HTTP session accumulation is possible in stateful session-based applications, but modern Spring Boot REST APIs are typically stateless (no HttpSession per request). Session objects also don't directly hold response body byte[] — the response is sent to the client and the buffer is typically released after the response completes. The cache pattern is more consistent with the described symptoms.

options.label: D
options.text: The PDF generation creates a new ClassLoader per request to isolate the PDF library. ClassLoaders are not garbage collected because Metaspace holds strong references to them, causing Metaspace exhaustion over time.
options.feedback: ClassLoader leaks manifest as OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace (not heap space) and are associated with dynamic class loading patterns (OSGi, plugin architectures, hot deployment). The error message 'Java heap space' specifically indicates heap exhaustion, not Metaspace. Additionally, new ClassLoaders per request is an unusual and extreme design choice unlikely in a standard PDF library integration.

stages.principalRationale: Symptom pattern recognition: (1) OOM in Java heap space → strong references preventing GC, not off-heap issue; (2) linear growth starting at a known feature release → the feature introduced the growing reference; (3) byte[] dominated heap dump → large object accumulation. These three data points together strongly indicate an unbounded cache of large objects.

stages.question: You open the OOM heap dump in Eclipse MAT. What analysis steps confirm the root cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the Leak Suspects report. It will automatically identify the unbounded cache and display the class name and stack trace where it was populated.
options.feedback: Eclipse MAT's Leak Suspects report is a useful starting point, but it performs heuristic analysis and may not identify the specific cache class clearly. It identifies 'accumulation points' by finding objects that retain large amounts of heap but cannot give the full context of why they are retained. The dominator tree analysis is more precise and actionable for cache-type leaks.

options.label: B
options.text: Open the Dominator Tree: sort retained heap descending. The dominator (object that, if removed, would free the most heap) will be the cache object. Inspect its type, retained size, and reference chain to identify: (a) the cache's class name, (b) which class holds a reference to the cache (GC root), (c) the type of objects in the cache (byte[]). Then use 'Path to GC Roots' on a sample byte[] to confirm the reference chain: GC Root → Cache → byte[].
options.feedback: Correct. The Dominator Tree identifies the largest retained-heap objects. For a cache leak, the cache object (HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap) will appear near the top, retaining a large fraction of total heap. 'Path to GC Roots' traces exactly why a specific byte[] is not collectable: the reference chain from the GC root (static field, Spring singleton bean) through the cache to the byte[]. This gives you the class name, field name, and code location to fix.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the Histogram view: sort by 'Shallow Heap' descending. Find byte[] at the top. This confirms the byte[] accumulation. The histogram gives you the total byte[] count and size.
options.feedback: The Histogram confirms byte[] accumulation (useful as a first validation step) but does not explain WHY the byte[] objects are retained. Without the Dominator Tree and GC Root analysis, you know what is using memory but not what is holding it live. The Dominator Tree is the tool that shows the retention chain and identifies the fix location.

options.label: D
options.text: Search the heap dump for instances of common cache classes: ConcurrentHashMap, Guava Cache, Caffeine Cache. If any instance retains > 100MB, it is the leaking cache.
options.feedback: Searching for specific cache class instances is a reasonable manual investigation step but requires knowing which cache libraries are in use and searching each one individually. The Dominator Tree approach is more systematic — it surfaces the largest memory holders regardless of their class type, without requiring prior knowledge of the caching mechanism used.

stages.principalRationale: Dominator Tree + Path to GC Roots is the standard methodology for heap dump analysis. The Dominator Tree identifies what is retaining the most memory; Path to GC Roots shows why it cannot be collected. Together they provide the class name, field name, and reference chain needed for a targeted fix.

stages.question: The analysis confirms: `PdfStatementService` has a static `Map<String, byte[]> statementCache` with no size limit. What is the correct fix and prevention strategy?

options.label: A
options.text: Replace the static Map with a Caffeine cache: `Cache<String, byte[]> cache = Caffeine.newBuilder().maximumSize(100).expireAfterAccess(10, MINUTES).build()`. The size limit and TTL prevent unbounded growth.
options.feedback: Correct. Caffeine with maximumSize and expireAfterAccess provides both size-based eviction (never more than 100 entries) and time-based eviction (removes entries inactive for 10 minutes). This eliminates unbounded growth while retaining the caching performance benefit for frequently requested statements. The fix is minimal — replace the Map reference with a Caffeine Cache and remove the static field (inject the cache via Spring @Bean instead of a static initialiser).

options.label: B
options.text: Remove the cache entirely. PDF generation is an I/O-bound operation; re-generating on each request is acceptable. Remove statementCache and generate the PDF on every GET /statements/{accountId} call.
options.feedback: Removing the cache is safe from a memory perspective but may introduce unacceptable latency for repeated requests. If PDF generation involves multiple database queries and report rendering (typical), uncached generation on every request could add 500ms–2s per call. Whether this is acceptable depends on the SLO. Caffeine with bounded size and TTL is better: it preserves performance benefit while adding safety bounds.

options.label: C
options.text: Use WeakReference<byte[]> as the cache value. WeakReferences are eligible for GC when memory pressure is high, allowing the GC to reclaim PDF bytes automatically.
options.feedback: WeakReferences allow GC to reclaim the referenced objects under memory pressure — but only after a full GC cycle determines memory is needed. In practice, WeakReference caches perform poorly: under steady load, GC constantly collects the cache entries (causing cache misses) or fails to collect fast enough under sudden load spikes (OOM still occurs). SoftReference (collected only before OOM) is better than WeakReference for caches, but Caffeine with explicit size limits is better than either reference type approach.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase -Xmx to 16GB. The cache will reach steady state once all account statements have been generated once and no new accounts are added.
options.feedback: Increasing heap without fixing the unbounded cache is a time-delay, not a fix. New accounts are constantly added; existing account statements may be regenerated due to new transactions. The cache will grow without bound regardless of heap size. This was already demonstrated by the team's previous increase from 2GB to 4GB — it only extended the OOM interval.

stages.principalRationale: Every cache in production must have an explicit maximum size and TTL. These are not performance optimisations — they are correctness constraints that prevent memory exhaustion. Caffeine is the standard Java caching library that provides both. The fix takes under 10 lines of code; the prevention strategy is a code review policy requiring all caches to have bounded configuration.

debrief.summary: Unbounded caches accumulating large objects are one of the most common causes of Java OOM in production. The diagnostic path is: OOM error → heap dump → Dominator Tree → Path to GC Roots. The fix is always: add explicit size limit and TTL to the cache using Caffeine. Prevention is a code review policy requiring bounded configuration on all caches.
keyTakeaways: OOM: Java heap space → strong references preventing GC, not off-heap native memory
Dominator Tree identifies the largest retained-heap holders; Path to GC Roots shows why they cannot be collected
Every production cache must have maximumSize and expireAfterAccess — no unbounded Maps
Caffeine is the standard Java caching library: use Caffeine.newBuilder().maximumSize(N).expireAfterAccess(T, UNIT).build()
Increasing heap without fixing the cache is a time-delay, not a solution
