scenarios.title: The Alert Fatigue
scenarios.subtitle: 420 PagerDuty Pages in One Week Hide a Real Outage
scenarios.context:
The payment processing team receives 420 PagerDuty pages in one week. 65% are P2 alerts for P99 latency > 500ms. P50 latency is healthy at 45ms. P99 is naturally spiky — GC pauses and 1–2% of slow downstream API calls push individual requests above 500ms even during normal operation.

Engineers begin muting P99 alerts during business hours. On Wednesday afternoon, a genuine 25-minute partial outage (40% of payments timing out) goes undetected for 25 minutes because the alert was lost in the noise. Customers escalate via Twitter. The engineering VP asks for a root-cause analysis of the monitoring failure.
systemConstraints: SLO: P99 latency < 200ms, 99.9% availability (monthly)
Current alert: P99 > 500ms for 1 consecutive minute → PagerDuty P2
Normal P99: 85ms median, spikes to 400-600ms for 2-3% of 1-minute windows
Outage P99: > 2,000ms for 25 consecutive minutes
Monthly error budget: 43.8 minutes of SLO-breaching downtime
Alert volume: 420 pages/week (65% false positive P99 alerts)
Prometheus + Grafana monitoring stack

stages.question: What is the fundamental flaw in the current alerting strategy that causes both the false positive storm and the missed real outage?

options.label: A
options.text: The P99 threshold (500ms) is too aggressive. Raising it to 2,000ms would eliminate the false positives and would have caught the genuine outage.
options.feedback: Raising the threshold to 2,000ms would have caught Wednesday's outage (P99 > 2,000ms) but would miss slower degradations that still breach the SLO. More importantly, threshold-based alerts on P99 have an inherent false positive rate due to natural variability — raising the threshold just shifts the threshold, it does not solve the underlying problem of threshold alerts not distinguishing transient spikes from sustained degradation.

options.label: B
options.text: Point-in-time threshold alerts fire on transient spikes that self-resolve without consuming meaningful error budget. A 1-minute P99 spike to 600ms consumes 1 minute of the 43.8-minute monthly budget but generates a PagerDuty page. Genuine outages also spike P99 — but they burn budget continuously. The alert does not distinguish between a 1-minute transient (1/43.8 = 2.3% budget) and a 25-minute sustained outage (57% budget). Both generate exactly one alert.
options.feedback: Exactly right. This is the fundamental problem with threshold alerting on point-in-time metrics. The alert does not encode the budget burn rate — it fires identically for a 1-minute spike and a 25-minute outage. The result is high false positive rate (spikes are common) with no additional urgency for genuine outages (same alert severity). Multi-window burn rate alerting solves this by linking alert severity to the rate of budget consumption.

options.label: C
options.text: P99 is the wrong SLI. Alerting on P50 (median) latency would have fewer false positives because the median is more stable.
options.feedback: P50 alerting would miss the 2% of slow requests that breach the SLO — it would not have caught Wednesday's outage (40% of payments timing out) until P50 was affected. SLOs are defined on the percentile that matters for user experience; dropping to P50 for alerting would create a monitoring gap for the slower tail of the distribution.

options.label: D
options.text: Too many teams are subscribed to the same alert. Alert routing should ensure only the on-call engineer is paged, reducing the perception of noise.
options.feedback: Alert routing affects who receives pages but not the number of pages generated. Even if only one engineer is paged, 420 pages/week is alert fatigue — the volume is the problem, not the distribution. The fix must reduce the number of alerts generated by improving the alerting strategy, not just narrow the recipient list.

stages.principalRationale: The core insight: threshold alerts fire on events, not on sustained budget burn. For SLO-based monitoring, what matters is not whether the SLO was briefly breached but how fast the error budget is being consumed. Multi-window burn rate alerting encodes this by measuring burn rate over both short and long windows simultaneously.

stages.question: What alerting strategy should replace the point-in-time P99 threshold alert?

options.label: A
options.text: Multi-window burn rate alerting: Page only when error budget is burning at a rate that would exhaust the monthly budget within X hours in BOTH a short window (1h) AND a long window (6h). The dual-window requirement filters transient spikes (burn high in 1h but not in 6h) from sustained degradation (burn high in both).
options.feedback: Correct. Multi-window burn rate alerting (from the Google SRE Workbook) uses two alert conditions: fast burn (1-hour window, high burn rate threshold — catches major outages quickly) and slow burn (6-hour window, lower burn rate threshold — catches sustained partial degradation). Both must fire simultaneously to page. A transient 2-minute spike burns fast in the 1h window but not in the 6h window — no page. Wednesday's 25-minute outage (40% timeout) burns fast in both windows — page. This directly solved the false positive problem.

options.label: B
options.text: Replace P99 latency alerting with error rate alerting: alert only on HTTP 5xx error rate > 1%. Errors are clearer signals than latency.
options.feedback: Error rate alerting is complementary to latency alerting but does not replace it. Many SLO-violating scenarios produce timeouts (long latency) without 5xx errors — the client gives up and the server returns 200 OK too slowly. Wednesday's outage (40% payments timing out) may have shown as timeouts before error responses. SLO definitions should include both error rate and latency as SLIs.

options.label: C
options.text: Increase the alert evaluation window from 1 minute to 15 minutes. Alert only if P99 > 500ms sustained for 15 consecutive minutes.
options.feedback: 15-minute sustained alerting would have caught Wednesday's 25-minute outage (barely — it fires at minute 15 of 25). But it would still generate false positives on any 15-minute degradation period. More importantly, a 15-minute detection delay for major outages is too slow for a payment system — the SLO budget for a 15-minute delay is 15/43.8 = 34% consumed before alerting. Multi-window burn rate provides both fast detection for severe outages and slow detection for gradual degradation.

options.label: D
options.text: Use anomaly detection: alert only when P99 deviates more than 3 standard deviations from the rolling 7-day average. This adapts to natural variability patterns.
options.feedback: Anomaly detection is useful for capacity planning and trend analysis but is a poor fit for SLO-based alerting. It requires significant historical data for calibration, can mask seasonal patterns as 'normal', and does not encode the budget burn concept. A 3σ deviation on a naturally variable metric like P99 tail latency produces many false positives or misses genuine outages that happen to fit the historical pattern.

stages.principalRationale: Multi-window burn rate alerting is the Google SRE recommendation for SLO-based alerting. The dual-window requirement (both short and long windows must fire) is the key innovation — it filters transient spikes while catching both fast burns (major outages) and slow burns (gradual degradation). This directly addresses the false positive storm while maintaining genuine outage detection.

stages.question: With multi-window burn rate alerting in place, the team asks: when should a new feature deployment be blocked due to error budget status?

options.label: A
options.text: Never block deployments based on error budget — the deployment pipeline should be independent of SLO status. Error budget management is a post-deployment concern.
options.feedback: If error budget is exhausted, every deployment that causes any additional unavailability exceeds the SLO commitment to customers. Deploying with zero remaining budget is a business decision — but it must be made explicitly, not by default. An error budget policy that blocks deployments when budget is low forces the team to treat availability as a first-class engineering metric, not an afterthought.

options.label: B
options.text: Define an error budget policy: (1) Budget > 50% remaining → deploy freely; (2) Budget 10–50% remaining → deploy with extra caution (canary, manual smoke test, rollback plan rehearsed); (3) Budget < 10% remaining → freeze all non-critical deployments, focus sprint on reliability improvements; (4) Budget exhausted → no deployments until next month's budget resets. Document and enforce as an engineering team policy.
options.feedback: Correct. The error budget policy converts the abstract SLO budget into concrete deployment decisions. It aligns product velocity (want to ship features) with reliability (must maintain SLO). Crucially, it is documented and enforced — not ad hoc. When budget is low, the team naturally pivots to reliability work (which is what the SLO framework is designed to incentivise). The tiered policy (50% / 10% / 0%) balances velocity preservation with risk management.

options.label: C
options.text: Block all deployments whenever the monthly error budget reaches < 50% with more than 15 days remaining in the month.
options.feedback: A single 50% threshold is too conservative for most engineering teams — 50% budget with 15 days remaining means you are on track, not in trouble. Tiered thresholds (freely / caution / freeze) allow velocity to continue when the situation is not dire, while enforcing genuine caution when budget is critically low. A fixed 50% block would generate excessive friction and may cause teams to game the SLO definition.

options.label: D
options.text: Track error budget in a weekly engineering review meeting. The team votes on whether to deploy based on current budget status.
options.feedback: Weekly reviews are too infrequent for fast-moving deployment pipelines. Teams may deploy dozens of times per week. A documented, automatically enforceable policy (checked in CI/CD gate) is more robust than a weekly meeting. The policy should be consistent and predictable, not subject to weekly team votes.

stages.principalRationale: Error budget policy is what transforms SLOs from abstract metrics into engineering team behaviour. The tiered policy (freely / caution / freeze / stop) is the standard Google SRE pattern. The key benefit: the team self-regulates deployment velocity based on reliability evidence, without requiring management intervention.

debrief.summary: Alert fatigue is a monitoring system failure, not a human failure. Point-in-time threshold alerts fire identically for transient spikes and genuine outages, creating signal-to-noise ratios that make monitoring useless. Multi-window burn rate alerting links alert severity to error budget consumption rate — only paging when the SLO is being meaningfully breached. The error budget policy operationalises the SLO into deployment decisions.
keyTakeaways: Point-in-time threshold alerts cannot distinguish transient spikes from sustained outages
Multi-window burn rate: page when budget burns fast in BOTH 1h window AND 6h window simultaneously
Fast burn catches major outages (P1); slow burn catches gradual degradation (P2)
Error budget policy converts abstract SLO budget into concrete deployment gate decisions
Alert fatigue → engineers mute alerts → real outages missed: a predictable, preventable failure mode
furtherReading: Track 08, Lesson 01 — SLOs, SLIs, Error Budgets
Track 08, Lesson 06 — Multi-Window Burn Rate Alerting
Track 13, Lesson 03 — Prometheus Alerting Rules for Financial Services

scenarios.title: The Config Disaster
scenarios.subtitle: Copy-Paste Error in Deployment Pipeline Causes 12,000 False Declines
scenarios.context:
At 09:12 on Monday, 12,000 customers are declined for payments in 45 minutes. The decline reason: FRAUD_SCORE_THRESHOLD_EXCEEDED. The fraud team investigates: `fraud_score_threshold` config changed from 0.75 to 0.075 in the last deployment. 99.8% of transactions score above 0.075 and are declined.

Root cause trace: a developer copy-pasted deployment config between environments. The staging config uses 0.075 (a testing value for triggering fraud alerts on test transactions). Production was supposed to retain 0.75. The copy-paste was not reviewed because config changes were bundled with the code change PR. No automated validation checked the config range before deployment.
systemConstraints: fraud_score_threshold: externally configured via Spring application.yml in the deployment artifact
Deployment: Kubernetes rolling deployment, all 12 pods updated within 4 minutes
Monitoring: fraud decline rate alert fires at > 5% decline rate. At 09:12, rate jumped to 99.8%.
Alert fired at 09:17 (5-minute evaluation window). Team diagnosed and rolled back by 09:57.
12,000 false declines in 45 minutes
Config is part of the application container image (baked in at build time)
No config schema validation step in CI/CD pipeline

stages.question: What are the two root causes of this incident — one technical, one process — and which is more important to fix first?

options.label: A
options.text: Technical: the fraud score threshold value is hardcoded in the application; it should be a database-driven configuration that can be changed without deployment. Process: developers need more training on deployment config management.
options.feedback: Database-driven configuration adds complexity and a new failure mode (database unavailable = service cannot start). Training is a low-leverage fix for a systematic process gap — the same error can be made by any developer, regardless of training. The technical root cause is lack of config validation; the process root cause is config and code bundled in the same review.

options.label: B
options.text: Technical: no schema validation on config values before deployment (fraud_score_threshold = 0.075 is not in the valid range [0.5, 1.0] but nothing prevented it from being deployed). Process: config changes were bundled with code changes in the same PR, reducing scrutiny on the config delta. Both must be fixed; the technical validation is the higher-leverage fix because it catches errors machines can detect before they reach production.
options.feedback: Correct on both counts and the prioritisation. Config schema validation is the technical control that prevents out-of-range values regardless of human error. Separating config changes from code changes (or requiring separate review) is the process control that increases scrutiny. Schema validation catches what humans miss; process separation ensures humans look. Technical controls scale better than process controls — schema validation catches every future typo, training cannot.

options.label: C
options.text: Technical: the alert evaluation window was 5 minutes, too slow to detect the fraud decline spike in real time. Process: on-call rotation should have an engineer monitoring dashboards during all deployments.
options.feedback: The 5-minute alert window is a valid concern (it contributed to 5 minutes of additional exposure before detection) but is not the root cause. Even a 1-minute alert would have caused ~1,000 false declines before detection. The root cause is that an invalid config value was deployed — faster detection reduces impact but does not prevent the incident. Config validation prevents it entirely.

options.label: D
options.text: Technical: Kubernetes rolled out all 12 pods within 4 minutes, too fast. A slower rolling deployment would have limited impact. Process: post-deployment verification should check the fraud decline rate before completing the rollout.
options.feedback: Slower rollout reduces impact (fewer pods affected before detection) and post-deployment verification is valuable — but neither addresses the root cause: an invalid config value entered the deployment artifact. Post-deployment verification is a mitigation; config schema validation is prevention. For a payment system, even 1 pod with an invalid fraud threshold causes unacceptable false declines.

stages.principalRationale: Root cause analysis must distinguish between causes (what allowed the error to occur) and mitigations (what limited its impact). Config schema validation is a cause-level fix: it prevents invalid values from being deployed. Alert speed and rollout speed are impact-limitation controls. Fix the cause first.

stages.question: What is the most effective technical control to prevent invalid config values from reaching production?

options.label: A
options.text: Move all config values to AWS Secrets Manager or Kubernetes ConfigMap managed by a separate team (platform engineering). Config changes require a separate ticket and approval process, adding a human review gate.
options.feedback: Separating config ownership (platform team approves config changes) adds a human review gate. Human gates slow down the deployment pipeline and do not scale — the platform team becomes a bottleneck. Human reviewers also miss errors that schema validation would catch (the platform team reviewer may not know that 0.075 is invalid for fraud_score_threshold). Schema validation provides stronger guarantees with less process overhead.

options.label: B
options.text: Config-as-code with machine-validated schema: define a JSON Schema or custom validator for each environment's config file. The CI pipeline runs config-schema-validate.sh before building the container image. For fraud_score_threshold, the schema defines: type: number, minimum: 0.5, maximum: 1.0. Any value outside this range fails the CI build before the image is built.
options.feedback: Correct. Config schema validation in CI is the technical control that closes the gap: it catches invalid values before the image is built, let alone deployed. The schema is source-controlled alongside the config (config-as-code), so the range constraint is visible to developers and enforced automatically. This catches typos, copy-paste errors, and value range errors that human reviewers miss. For financial config values (thresholds, limits, rate limits), schema validation is mandatory.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a Spring Boot application startup check: in @PostConstruct, validate that fraud_score_threshold is between 0.5 and 1.0. If invalid, throw a BeanCreationException that prevents the application from starting.
options.feedback: Application startup validation is better than no validation — it prevents the pod from starting with an invalid config, which is better than deploying and causing false declines. However, Kubernetes rolling deployment would launch the new pod, it would fail to start, Kubernetes would detect the crash loop and stop the rollout, and the existing pods (with the old config) would continue serving traffic. This catches the error at deployment time — but CI validation catches it even earlier (before the image is even built), which is better.

options.label: D
options.text: Encrypt all config values in the deployment artifact. Only the production deployment pipeline can decrypt them, ensuring staging config cannot be copy-pasted to production.
options.feedback: Encryption prevents viewing config values but does not prevent deploying wrong values. A developer who encrypts 0.075 with the production key has successfully deployed an invalid value that is now encrypted. Encryption addresses confidentiality, not config value correctness.

stages.principalRationale: Shift config validation left: catch errors in CI before the image is built, not after deployment when customers are affected. Schema-defined constraints for business-critical config values (thresholds, limits) are non-negotiable in financial systems.

stages.question: Config validation is in place. What deployment pattern provides the fastest detection of any unexpected production behaviour (including config values that pass schema validation but are still wrong)?

options.label: A
options.text: Blue-green deployment: deploy the new version to a separate environment, run smoke tests, then switch all traffic at once. Roll back by switching traffic back.
options.feedback: Blue-green eliminates gradual rollout risk but puts all traffic onto the new version simultaneously after the switch. If the smoke tests miss the config issue (which is likely for edge cases), 100% of traffic is affected from the first second of the switch. It also requires running two full production environments simultaneously, which doubles infrastructure cost.

options.label: B
options.text: Canary deployment: route 1% of traffic to the new version for 15 minutes. Monitor fraud decline rate on the canary vs baseline. Automated rollback if decline rate on canary exceeds baseline by > 5%. If canary passes, progressively increase to 10%, 25%, 100% with the same gates between each step.
options.feedback: Correct. A canary deployment limits the blast radius of any undiscovered issue to the canary traffic percentage (1% → 12,000 customers becomes 120 customers). The automated comparison (canary decline rate vs. baseline) catches statistical anomalies in the new version without requiring engineers to manually interpret dashboards. Progressive rollout (1% → 10% → 25% → 100%) with automated gates is the industry-standard deployment pattern for high-risk production changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Feature flags: deploy the new config but keep the old fraud threshold active. Enable the new config via a feature flag for 0.1% of users. Monitor for 24 hours before full rollout.
options.feedback: Feature flags for config values are complex to implement correctly (the flag logic must be in the fraud service, not just the config) and 24-hour monitoring windows significantly slow deployment velocity. For a config value like a fraud threshold, a canary deployment achieves the same safety goal with a 15-minute observation window rather than 24 hours.

options.label: D
options.text: Shadow mode: run the new fraud scoring logic in parallel with the old logic for 1 hour, logging both decisions. Deploy the new logic to production only if the shadow decisions match the old ones within 2%.
options.feedback: Shadow mode (dual-running and comparing results) is excellent for ML model validation and algorithm changes. For a config value change (threshold adjustment), it is overkill — the purpose of changing the threshold is precisely to change the decision rate. A shadow comparison would flag the threshold change as a 'mismatch' and block the deployment even when the change is intentional. Canary with business metric monitoring is more appropriate.

stages.principalRationale: Canary deployments limit blast radius while providing real production signal. The comparison-based automated gate (canary vs baseline) is what distinguishes a good canary from a simple gradual rollout — it surfaces problems without requiring manual interpretation. For financial services where configuration errors can cause thousands of customer-impacting decisions in minutes, canary with automated comparison is the deployment safety standard.

debrief.summary: Configuration errors are a leading cause of production incidents in modern deployment pipelines. The defence-in-depth approach: (1) schema validation in CI catches invalid values before the image is built; (2) application startup validation catches values that pass schema but fail business rules; (3) canary deployment limits blast radius for anything that passes both validation layers. Schema validation is the highest-leverage control — it scales automatically to every deployment.
keyTakeaways: Config schema validation in CI is the highest-leverage control: catches errors before the image is built
Config-as-code: define allowed ranges/values in a schema that is source-controlled and machine-validated
Application @PostConstruct validation is a secondary defence for business-rule constraints not expressible in schema
Canary deployment with automated comparison (canary vs baseline) limits blast radius to 1% of users
Never bundle config changes with code changes in the same PR — config changes deserve separate scrutiny

Track 01, Lesson 07 — Configuration Management and Deployment Safety
Track 08, Lesson 09 — Deployment Verification and Automated Rollback

scenarios.title: The Slow Query Bomb
scenarios.subtitle: Billing Job Takes 4 Minutes in Staging, 6+ Hours in Production
scenarios.context:
The monthly billing job runs fine in staging: 50,000 customers, completes in 4 minutes. First production run with 8.2 million customers has been running for 6 hours without completing. The core query:

```sql
SELECT c.id, c.email, SUM(t.amount) as total_billed
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN transactions t ON c.id = t.customer_id
WHERE t.created_at >= '2026-10-01'
  AND c.billing_status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.id, c.email
```

Staging and production have identical schemas. The query runs in 4 minutes against the 50k staging dataset. The DBA ran EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on production and found: Seq Scan on transactions (cost=0 rows=312,847,000). No index is being used for the join or date filter.
systemConstraints: customers table: 8.2M rows (production), 50k rows (staging)
transactions table: 312M rows (production), 1.5M rows (staging)
Existing indexes: customers(id) PRIMARY KEY, transactions(id) PRIMARY KEY, customers(billing_status)
No index on transactions(customer_id) or transactions(created_at)
PostgreSQL query planner statistics: last ANALYZE ran 3 days ago on production
Staging: PostgreSQL shares same instance, different database, full ANALYZE runs nightly
transactions table size: ~160GB

stages.question: Why did the same query perform acceptably in staging but catastrophically in production?

options.label: A
options.text: Production PostgreSQL is under higher concurrent load from OLTP queries, starving the billing job of I/O bandwidth.
options.feedback: Concurrent load contributes to I/O contention but does not explain a 90× performance difference (4 min vs 6+ hours). If concurrent load were the primary factor, the query plan would still use indexes. The EXPLAIN output shows a sequential scan — meaning the planner chose not to use indexes, regardless of concurrent load. The query plan choice is the primary driver.

options.label: B
options.text: In staging (1.5M transactions), PostgreSQL's planner estimated that an index scan on transactions(customer_id) was cheaper than a seq scan and chose the index. In production (312M transactions, 160GB), without an index on customer_id, the planner has no choice but to do a full sequential scan. Additionally, without statistics from a recent ANALYZE on the production transactions table, the planner's row estimates are inaccurate — compounding the problem. A full 160GB seq scan for a join is catastrophic at scale.
options.feedback: Correct. The query plan is data-volume-dependent. At 1.5M staging rows, PostgreSQL may execute the query quickly even with suboptimal plans (small tables fit in shared_buffers). At 312M production rows, the absence of an index on transactions(customer_id) forces a 160GB sequential scan for every customer lookup. Stale statistics compound the issue: the planner's estimates are wrong, potentially choosing worse join strategies. This is a classic case of 'works in staging, fails in production' due to dataset size differences.

options.label: C
options.text: Production PostgreSQL has a different max_parallel_workers_per_gather setting, disabling the parallel query execution that made staging fast.
options.feedback: Parallel query settings affect throughput but do not cause a 90× difference on their own. Even with parallel workers, a 160GB sequential scan takes many minutes. The root cause is the absence of an index on the join column — no parallelism setting compensates for a missing index on a 312M-row join.

options.label: D
options.text: The transactions table is not partitioned in production, causing table bloat and lock contention during the monthly billing scan.
options.feedback: Partitioning would help this query significantly (partition pruning on created_at) but its absence does not explain the staging vs production difference — staging also has an unpartitioned transactions table. The difference is the data volume and the absence of a suitable index.

stages.principalRationale: Query plans are data-dependent. A plan that is acceptable on a small dataset becomes catastrophic on a large one. Always test query plans against production-sized datasets — not just staging. The EXPLAIN output is the diagnostic tool, not performance timing.

stages.question: What index strategy resolves the immediate problem, and what longer-term architectural change should be considered?

options.label: A
options.text: Index on transactions(created_at) only. The WHERE clause filters by created_at first, reducing the rows before the join.
options.feedback: An index on created_at alone helps the date filter but does not help the join. After filtering by date, PostgreSQL still needs to find each customer's transactions — without an index on customer_id, this requires a scan of the filtered set for each customer, which is still slow at scale. The join column index is more important than the filter column index for this query pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: Composite index on transactions(customer_id, created_at): covers both the join condition (customer_id) and the date filter (created_at). PostgreSQL can use this for an Index Scan or Index Only Scan. Confirm with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) that the plan changes from Seq Scan to Index Scan. Run ANALYZE on the transactions table first to update planner statistics.
options.feedback: Correct. The composite index on (customer_id, created_at) covers both the join condition and the WHERE filter. For each customer, PostgreSQL uses the index to efficiently find their transactions within the date range — an Index Range Scan instead of a full sequential scan. Running ANALYZE first updates the planner's statistics, ensuring it makes correct cardinality estimates for the new plan. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) post-index confirms the plan change.

options.label: C
options.text: Partition the transactions table by created_at (monthly). The billing query automatically benefits from partition pruning, scanning only the October partition.
options.feedback: Partitioning is an excellent long-term architectural improvement — it enables partition pruning (only scanning the relevant month's data) and simplifies data retention. However, partitioning a 160GB live table is a multi-hour online migration project, not an immediate fix. The composite index can be added with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (non-blocking) in minutes, restoring acceptable query performance immediately.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the billing job to run against a dedicated read replica with higher shared_buffers and work_mem, reducing contention with the OLTP primary.
options.feedback: Running analytics on a read replica is a good operational practice (reduces primary load), but it does not fix the missing index. The read replica has the same schema and the same absence of indexes — the same 160GB sequential scan would occur on the replica. Add the index first; then migrate to replica for operational isolation.

stages.principalRationale: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on (customer_id, created_at) is a non-blocking operation that can be added to a live 160GB table without downtime. It directly fixes the query plan from seq scan to index range scan. Combined with ANALYZE, it restores the query to acceptable performance immediately — the longer-term architectural improvements (partitioning, read replica) can follow.

stages.question: How do you ensure this category of problem — query plan regression at production scale — does not recur for future billing queries?

options.label: A
options.text: Run EXPLAIN on all billing queries as part of code review. If the plan shows a Seq Scan, require an index before merging.
options.feedback: Manual EXPLAIN review in code review is a step in the right direction but has limitations: reviewers may not have access to production-sized data to test against, Seq Scan on a small table may be correct (not all Seq Scans are problems), and code review is easy to skip under deadline pressure. Automated testing against production-scale data provides stronger guarantees.

options.label: B
options.text: Automated query plan regression testing in CI: run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on the top N billing queries against a production-anonymised dataset (or a statistical sample). Assert that the plan contains no Seq Scan on tables > 10M rows. Alert if any plan changes from Index Scan to Seq Scan between deployments.
options.feedback: Correct. Automated query plan tests with production-scale data catch regressions before they reach production. The assertion (no Seq Scan on large tables) provides a clear pass/fail gate. Comparing plans between deployments (is the plan worse than before?) detects regressions introduced by schema or data distribution changes. This requires maintaining a production-scale test dataset, which is an infrastructure investment justified by preventing 6-hour billing failures.

options.label: C
options.text: Set statement_timeout = '10 minutes' on the billing job connection. If a query exceeds 10 minutes, it fails fast rather than running indefinitely.
options.feedback: Timeouts are a safety valve, not a prevention strategy. A 10-minute timeout would have terminated the billing job after 10 minutes — but the billing still would not have completed. Customers would not have been billed. The goal is to fix the query, not to fail it faster.

options.label: D
options.text: Run ANALYZE on all large tables before the monthly billing job. Fresh statistics ensure the planner makes correct decisions.
options.feedback: Running ANALYZE before the billing job ensures fresh statistics, which helps the planner make better decisions. But it does not prevent the missing-index problem: even with perfect statistics, the planner cannot use an index that does not exist. Fresh statistics on a table with a full sequential scan means the planner knows exactly how many rows it is scanning — it still must scan them all.

stages.principalRationale: Query plan regression testing against production-scale data is the only reliable way to catch this category of bug before it reaches production. The investment (maintaining a production-scale test dataset) pays for itself after the first prevented incident.

debrief.summary: Missing indexes on join columns are invisible at small dataset sizes and catastrophic at production scale. Query performance testing must use production-representative data volumes. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) is the diagnostic tool — it shows the plan, not just the execution time. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY adds indexes to live tables without downtime.
keyTakeaways: Query plans are data-volume-dependent — staging performance does not predict production performance
Missing index on join column = full sequential scan on the joined table for every row in the driving table
Composite index (customer_id, created_at) covers both join condition and date filter
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY: non-blocking index creation on live tables — does not lock the table
Run ANALYZE after creating an index to give the planner accurate statistics for the new index
Automated EXPLAIN regression testing against production-scale data prevents recurrence

scenarios.title: The API Breaking Change
scenarios.subtitle: Silent Breaking Change in Payment API Breaks Four Mobile Clients
scenarios.context:
The payments API v1 has been live for 18 months. It returns:
```json
{ "status": "SUCCESS", "amount": 100.00, "reference": "PAY-123" }
```
The team deploys a new version that improves the response:
```json
{ "status": "COMPLETED", "amount": "100.00", "currency": "GBP", "reference": "PAY-123" }
```
Changes: (1) `status` value renamed from `SUCCESS` to `COMPLETED`, (2) `amount` type changed from JSON number to JSON string, (3) `currency` field added.

Three days after deployment, four mobile clients report broken apps: iOS app crashes on amount parsing (expects double, gets string), Android app shows incorrect payment status (checks for `SUCCESS` string), partner bank integration fails (amount field validation). No internal tests failed pre-deployment.
systemConstraints: API consumed by: iOS app (Swift Codable, strict type mapping), Android app (Kotlin data class), partner bank (OpenAPI schema validation), internal dashboard (JavaScript, flexible parsing)
No API versioning strategy — single endpoint /payments/{id}
No consumer-driven contract tests
Deployment: deployed as a single breaking release, no migration path
Mobile app release cycle: 2-4 weeks for App Store/Play Store approval
Partner bank integration: cannot deploy emergency fix without 48h change window

stages.question: Which of the three changes is a breaking change, and why did internal tests not catch them?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the status rename (SUCCESS → COMPLETED) is breaking. Changing amount from number to string is backward compatible in JSON because all numbers are representable as strings. Adding currency is an additive change and is always backward compatible.
options.feedback: All three changes are potentially breaking. Changing amount from JSON number (100.00) to JSON string ('100.00') breaks strictly-typed clients: Swift's Codable cannot map a JSON string to a Double field, and OpenAPI schema validation rejects the wrong type. The status rename breaks exact-string comparisons. Adding a required currency field can break clients that validate the response structure for unexpected fields.

options.label: B
options.text: All three changes are breaking for some clients: (1) status rename breaks exact-string comparison in Android; (2) amount type change (number → string) breaks typed deserialisers in iOS and OpenAPI schema validation in partner bank; (3) currency field addition can break clients that use strict schema validation rejecting unexpected fields. Internal tests did not catch these because tests only tested the server's output — no tests validated the response from the client's parsing perspective (consumer perspective).
options.feedback: Correct. Breaking changes must be evaluated from the consumer's perspective, not the producer's. A change that the server can make freely may break clients with typed deserialisers, exact-value comparisons, or strict schema validation. Internal tests (server-side assertions on the new format) confirm the server works — they cannot detect that clients are expecting the old format. Consumer-driven contract testing exists precisely to close this gap.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the amount type change is breaking. Status renames and new fields are always backward compatible per the OpenAPI specification.
options.feedback: OpenAPI spec allows field additions as backward compatible, but the spec describes the server's output — not the client's parsing behaviour. Clients that check status == 'SUCCESS' in their business logic are broken by the rename regardless of OpenAPI compatibility. The OpenAPI spec does not govern client code — consumer-driven contracts do.

options.label: D
options.text: None of the changes are technically breaking — the response is still valid JSON. Client applications should use defensive parsing that handles type variations and new fields gracefully.
options.feedback: Defensive parsing is an aspirational client design principle, not a guarantee. Typed deserialisers in modern mobile languages (Swift, Kotlin, TypeScript) provide type safety precisely by rejecting unexpected types — that is their feature, not a bug. API providers cannot require clients to implement defensive parsing as a prerequisite for backward compatibility. The API contract must be stable.

stages.principalRationale: Breaking changes are determined by what clients actually do with the response, not by what the API spec says is compatible. Consumer-driven contract testing captures the client's actual expectations and fails CI if the provider breaks them — before deployment.

stages.question: What versioning and evolution strategy prevents this class of problem for the payment API?

options.label: A
options.text: Semantic versioning in a response header: X-API-Version: 2.0.0. Clients that need the old format add an Accept-Version: 1.x.x header. The server serves the appropriate format based on the Accept-Version header.
options.feedback: Header-based versioning works but requires all clients to understand and implement the Accept-Version header — a client that does not send the header gets the latest version and may break. Mobile clients that are deployed and cannot be updated quickly would need to be updated to send the header before the server deploys the new version — still a coordination problem. URL-based versioning (v1/ vs v2/) is more explicit and easier to route.

options.label: B
options.text: URL-based API versioning (/v1/payments/{id} and /v2/payments/{id}) with a 90-day deprecation window: v1 is maintained alongside v2. Breaking changes only appear in a new version path. Clients migrate to v2 at their own pace within the deprecation window. Automated contract tests verify v1 response shape never changes. v1 is decommissioned only after all consumers have migrated.
options.feedback: Correct. URL-based versioning is explicit (clients choose their version), easy to route (API gateway or separate handler per version), and allows clients with long release cycles (mobile apps, partner banks) to migrate at their pace. The 90-day deprecation window accommodates the mobile app 2–4 week App Store cycle with 2–3 release iterations for migration. Automated contract tests ensuring v1 shape never changes are the enforcement mechanism.

options.label: C
options.text: Never introduce breaking changes — only extend the API additively (add fields, never rename or remove). Keep status as SUCCESS and add a statusV2: COMPLETED field. Keep amount as a number and add amountString: '100.00'.
options.feedback: Additive-only evolution is an admirable constraint but is not always practical. Renaming status values, correcting type mistakes, and removing deprecated fields are legitimate API evolution operations. The 'additive only' rule prevents necessary breaking changes and leads to APIs cluttered with deprecated dual-representation fields. Versioning provides a clean migration path without requiring permanent backward-compat shims.

options.label: D
options.text: Publish the API as an OpenAPI schema and require all consumers to validate their client code against the schema in their own CI pipelines. Schema changes are notified to consumers before deployment.
options.feedback: OpenAPI schema distribution and notification is a useful communication mechanism but relies on consumers proactively updating their tests when the schema changes. Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) inverts this: consumers publish their expectations; the provider CI validates against all consumer expectations before deployment. This is more reliable than notification-based coordination.

stages.principalRationale: URL-based versioning with deprecation windows is the most common and practical API versioning strategy for financial APIs with heterogeneous consumer populations (mobile apps, partner banks, internal services) with different deployment velocities.

stages.question: URL versioning is in place. What testing technique prevents breaking changes from being deployed to any version without being caught in CI?

options.label: A
options.text: Integration tests in the payment API's own test suite that validate the response format against expected JSON schemas. If the schema changes, the test fails.
options.feedback: Provider-side schema tests validate the server's output but only validate what the team writing the server thinks the response should look like. They cannot capture what clients actually do with the response — a schema test might pass for the new COMPLETED status while the Android client still expects SUCCESS. This is the same gap that caused the original incident.

options.label: B
options.text: Pact consumer-driven contract testing: each consumer (iOS app, Android app, partner bank) publishes a contract (Pact file) describing their actual request/response expectations. The payment API's CI runs pact-verify against all published consumer contracts. If the payment API response no longer satisfies any consumer contract, CI fails before the change is deployed.
options.feedback: Correct. Pact inverts the testing relationship: consumers define what they need; the provider verifies it delivers that. When the iOS team adds parsing for amount as Double, their Pact contract records this expectation. When the payment API tries to change amount to String, pact-verify fails CI — the iOS contract is violated. This catches breaking changes before deployment, regardless of which team made the change. Consumer contracts are versioned alongside the consumer code.

options.label: C
options.text: End-to-end integration tests that run all client apps against the payment API in a staging environment before each deployment.
options.feedback: End-to-end tests with real client apps are valuable for final verification but are slow (require building and deploying all client apps), expensive to maintain, and cannot run mobile apps in CI without a device farm. They also require coordination between teams — mobile apps must have a CI-deployable test build ready. Pact contract tests run as unit tests in each team's CI pipeline, with no coordination required.

options.label: D
options.text: API documentation review: require an engineering manager to approve all API changes after reviewing the change log against the list of known consumers.
options.feedback: Manual review by a manager is the lowest-leverage control — it relies on human memory of all consumer dependencies, is a bottleneck in the deployment pipeline, and misses implicit dependencies (undocumented internal consumers). Automated contract testing scales to any number of consumers without review bottlenecks.

stages.principalRationale: Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) is the standard solution for this problem. It captures consumer expectations as executable tests, runs them on every provider CI build, and catches breaking changes before deployment — without requiring the provider team to maintain a comprehensive list of all consumers and their expectations.

debrief.summary: API breaking changes are determined by consumer behaviour, not server output. Provider-side tests only validate the server's perspective. Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) captures each consumer's actual expectations and verifies them against every provider deployment. URL-based versioning with deprecation windows allows breaking changes to be introduced safely without requiring simultaneous client updates.
keyTakeaways: Breaking changes: type changes, value renames, field removals — evaluated from consumer parsing perspective
URL versioning (/v1/, /v2/) with 90-day deprecation window is the standard for heterogeneous consumer populations
Pact consumer-driven contracts: consumers publish expectations; provider CI verifies them before deployment
Mobile app release cycles (2-4 weeks) require long deprecation windows — plan accordingly
Adding fields is usually backward-compatible; renaming values and changing types are always breaking
furtherReading: Track 01, Lesson 10 — API Design and Evolution Patterns
Track 02, Lesson 12 — Distributed System Contracts and Compatibility
Track 12, Lesson 09 — Deployment Pipelines and Consumer-Driven Testing

scenarios.title: The Audit Gap
scenarios.subtitle: 5-Year Regulatory Audit Request Reveals 3.5 Years of Missing Records
scenarios.context:
The FCA requests all actions on 47 high-risk customer accounts for a 5-year period. The compliance team runs the extraction. 23 of the 47 accounts have missing records: audit events exist for the last 18 months but nothing before.

Investigation reveals: an archive job was scheduled to move audit records older than 90 days from PostgreSQL to S3. The job was designed as DELETE-then-S3-write (delete from DB first, then write to S3). 18 months ago, an IAM permission change broke the S3 write. The job logged a WARNING (not an ERROR) and continued. Records were deleted from PostgreSQL but never written to S3. No reconciliation check verified the archive. The gap covers 3.5 years of audit data.
systemConstraints: audit_events table: PostgreSQL, 90-day hot retention
Archive target: S3 bucket, 5-year retention policy
Archive job: runs nightly at 01:00, deletes records > 90 days from PostgreSQL, writes to S3
Failure mode: S3 write silently failed (WARNING log) for 18 months
Missing data: 23 accounts × ~3.5 years = estimated 50,000+ missing audit events
Regulatory requirement: FATF Recommendation 11 — 5-year retention of transaction records
On-call alert: none configured for archive job failures

stages.question: What is the root cause of the data loss, and what design principle was violated?

options.label: A
options.text: The IAM permission change was not tested. A proper change management process would have included testing S3 write permissions before the IAM change was applied.
options.feedback: Inadequate change management testing contributed to the initial breakage. However, the more fundamental issue is the archive job's design: it deleted records before confirming successful S3 write. Even perfect change management cannot prevent all permission changes from breaking archive jobs over a 5-year period. The design must be resilient to failures — which means write-then-delete, not delete-then-write.

options.label: B
options.text: The archive job violated the write-first principle: it deleted records from the source (PostgreSQL) before confirming successful write to the destination (S3). The S3 failure was treated as non-fatal (WARNING) with no stop-and-alert behaviour. Combined with no post-archive reconciliation (verify source count equals destination count), the failure was invisible for 18 months. The correct principle: never delete from source until destination write is confirmed and verified.
options.feedback: Correct. This is a data durability design failure. The delete-then-write pattern is irreversible: once records are deleted, the source of truth is gone. The correct pattern is write-first: (1) write to S3, (2) verify S3 object count matches source count, (3) only delete from PostgreSQL if verification passes, (4) alert and abort if S3 write fails — never delete. The 'treat S3 failure as WARNING and continue' decision compounded the error by silently destroying data.

options.label: C
options.text: S3 bucket versioning was not enabled. With versioning enabled, deleted objects would be retained as delete markers, allowing recovery.
options.feedback: S3 bucket versioning would not help here: the objects were never written to S3 in the first place. Versioning only retains overwritten or deleted objects that were previously written. Enabling versioning is a good defence against accidental deletion of S3 objects, but it cannot recover records that never reached S3.

options.label: D
options.text: PostgreSQL table partitioning was not set up. With partitioning, old partitions could be detached (not deleted) and retained locally, providing a secondary source of truth.
options.feedback: Partition detachment (instead of DELETE) is a valid retention strategy for PostgreSQL and would have preserved the data locally. However, it does not address the broader design problem: the archive job had no verification step and treated archive failure as non-fatal. Even with partitioned data, the design principle (write-first, verify, then delete/detach) must be maintained.

stages.principalRationale: Data migration and archiving must be designed with the write-first principle: the destination is confirmed before the source is modified. This principle extends to all data movement operations in financial systems. Treating a data destruction failure as a WARNING rather than a FATAL error is the deeper design failure.

stages.question: Redesign the archive job with correct durability guarantees. What is the correct implementation?

options.label: A
options.text: Write-first with atomic swap: (1) Write batch of audit records to S3 as a Parquet file; (2) Verify S3 object is readable and row count matches the batch; (3) Only if verification passes: DELETE the records from PostgreSQL; (4) If S3 write or verification fails: abort the batch, log ERROR, page on-call via PagerDuty, and DO NOT delete. Run nightly reconciliation: compare PostgreSQL record counts (by date range) against S3 object manifests — alert on any discrepancy.
options.feedback: Correct. This implements the write-first principle with explicit verification and hard failure on S3 errors. The reconciliation step provides ongoing assurance: even if the job logic has a bug, the nightly reconciliation catches count discrepancies before they accumulate for 18 months. The on-call alert converts a silent failure into a detected incident within 24 hours.

options.label: B
options.text: Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to automatically replicate S3 objects to a second bucket. If the primary S3 write fails, records are still in PostgreSQL and CRR will eventually replicate them.
options.feedback: Cross-Region Replication replicates objects that ARE written to S3 — it cannot recover objects that were never written. The problem is the initial S3 write failure, not replication. CRR does not help here.

options.label: C
options.text: Use PostgreSQL logical replication to stream changes to an S3-backed data lake (via Debezium and Kafka Connect). Records are streamed in real-time before the 90-day PostgreSQL retention expires.
options.feedback: CDC-based streaming archival is a robust architecture for financial audit data: it eliminates the batch archive job entirely and provides near-real-time S3 durability. This is better than the batch approach for new data. However, it requires significant infrastructure investment (Debezium + Kafka Connect) and does not solve the existing 50,000+ missing events. It is an architectural improvement, not an immediate remediation.

options.label: D
options.text: Extend PostgreSQL retention from 90 days to 5 years, eliminating the archive job entirely. Use PostgreSQL partitioning to manage table size.
options.feedback: Eliminating the archive job removes the failure mode. However, 5 years of audit data in PostgreSQL at current ingestion rates would be a multi-terabyte table requiring significant storage and backup infrastructure investment. S3 is the correct long-term storage for cold audit data. Fixing the archive job design is more cost-effective than retaining 5 years in PostgreSQL.

stages.principalRationale: Write-first + verify + alert is the correct pattern for all data migration jobs that touch regulatory data. The nightly reconciliation is the independent verification layer that catches any bugs in the job logic before they cause unrecoverable data loss.

stages.question: Beyond the archive job fix, what architectural pattern provides the strongest evidence to regulators that the audit trail is complete and has not been tampered with?

options.label: A
options.text: Store a daily checksum of all audit records per account in a separate table. Regulators can verify that the checksum matches the provided records.
options.feedback: Daily checksums per account provide some integrity assurance but can be faked by an adversary who also modifies the checksum table. The checksum and the data are stored in the same system and subject to the same access controls. A tamper-evident hash chain, where each record depends on all previous records, is significantly harder to falsify — modifying any record requires recalculating all subsequent hashes.

options.label: B
options.text: Hash-chained audit log: each audit record stores event_hash = SHA-256(event_type + payload + actor + previous_hash). A verification job runs weekly, recomputing the chain from the genesis record. Any deletion, modification, or insertion into the chain breaks the hash sequence, providing cryptographic evidence of tampering. The chain spans from PostgreSQL through S3 archives — the last PostgreSQL record's hash is included in the S3 archive manifest.
options.feedback: Correct. The hash chain provides cryptographic tamper evidence: modifying any record changes its hash, which changes all subsequent hashes. An independent verification job can confirm the chain is intact without access to the original writer. The chain continuity across the PostgreSQL-to-S3 boundary (via archive manifest) ensures the transition point cannot be a tampering vector. This is the standard pattern for FATF-compliant financial audit trails.

options.label: C
options.text: Use PostgreSQL row-level security to prevent DBA-level UPDATE or DELETE on the audit_events table. Only INSERT is permitted for the application role.
options.feedback: Row-level security preventing modifications is an important access control layer — it raises the bar for insider tampering. However, a superuser (which DBAs typically have) can bypass RLS. For regulatory evidence, cryptographic proof (hash chain) is stronger than access control proof because it can be independently verified without trusting the access control system. Both controls should be used together: RLS prevents casual modification; hash chain detects sophisticated tampering.

options.label: D
options.text: Write audit records to an immutable write-once S3 bucket with Object Lock enabled (WORM — Write Once Read Many). Once written, records cannot be deleted or modified for the retention period.
options.feedback: S3 Object Lock provides immutability at the storage layer — excellent for preventing deletion. However, it protects against deletion but not against writing incorrect records in the first place. A malicious actor could write fabricated audit records that are then immutably locked. Object Lock complements the hash chain: Object Lock prevents deletion; the hash chain proves the records that do exist are authentic and unmodified.

stages.principalRationale: Hash chaining is the gold standard for tamper-evident financial audit trails. It provides cryptographic, independently-verifiable proof that records have not been modified, deleted, or inserted after the fact. Combined with Object Lock (deletion prevention) and RLS (access control), it provides defence-in-depth for regulatory compliance.

debrief.summary: Data archiving for regulatory compliance is a financial operations problem, not just an infrastructure task. The write-first principle prevents data loss; hash chaining provides tamper evidence; nightly reconciliation provides ongoing assurance. Any job that deletes regulatory data must treat failure as fatal and alert immediately.
keyTakeaways: Write-first principle: confirm destination write before deleting from source — always, for regulatory data
Archive job failures must be FATAL, not WARNING — data destruction must never proceed silently
Nightly reconciliation: compare source counts against destination counts — catches bugs before 18 months pass
Hash chain: SHA-256(payload + previous_hash) = cryptographic tamper evidence across the full retention period
FATF Recommendation 11: 5-year retention — design for this from day one, not as an afterthought
furtherReading: Track 07, Lesson 08 — Compliance Data Architecture: Hot, Warm, Cold
Track 10, Lesson 12 — Tamper-Evident Data Patterns

scenarios.title: The Split Brain
scenarios.subtitle: Network Partition in Active-Active Banking Platform Creates Conflicting Balances
scenarios.context:
Active-active banking platform: London (3 CockroachDB nodes) and Frankfurt (3 CockroachDB nodes), 6-node Raft cluster. At 14:30, a fibre cut causes a full network partition between regions. Both regions continue serving their local traffic.

At 15:45, the partition heals. CockroachDB begins resolving. The operations team observes 3 accounts in the conflict resolution log with inconsistent balances. Account A shows £1,200 in London's view and £800 in Frankfurt's view. The head of risk asks: 'I thought CockroachDB with Raft consensus was split-brain resistant. How did we get conflicting balances?'
systemConstraints: CockroachDB 6 nodes: eu-west-1a, eu-west-1b, eu-west-1c (London), eu-central-1a, eu-central-1b, eu-central-1c (Frankfurt)
Raft quorum: 4 of 6 nodes required for leaseholder writes
Account tables: REGIONAL BY ROW — account rows homed to their owner's primary region
Kafka MirrorMaker 2: bidirectional replication for event topics
Cross-region Saga in progress at 14:30: London debit (step 1 completed), Frankfurt credit (step 2 pending)
Partition duration: 75 minutes
CockroachDB GLOBAL tables (payment_transactions): writes paused in Frankfurt during partition (no quorum)

stages.question: How did 3 accounts develop conflicting balances despite CockroachDB using Raft consensus?

options.label: A
options.text: CockroachDB's Raft implementation has a bug that allows split-brain writes. With 6 nodes split 3-3, both sides incorrectly believe they have quorum and accept writes independently.
options.feedback: CockroachDB's Raft implementation is well-tested and does not allow dual-quorum in a 6-node split 3-3. With 4-of-6 quorum requirement and a 3-3 split, neither side has quorum — both would refuse leaseholder writes. This is not a CockroachDB bug. The conflict has a different cause related to the REGIONAL BY ROW data layout.

options.label: B
options.text: REGIONAL BY ROW pins each account row's leaseholder to its home region. During the partition: London-homed accounts had their leaseholders in London (3 nodes have quorum if no cross-region ranges are involved for single-region rows). Frankfurt-homed accounts had their leaseholders in Frankfurt. Both regions had quorum for their home-region rows and accepted writes independently. The 3 conflicting accounts were involved in a cross-region Saga (step 1: London debit committed; step 2: Frankfurt credit was orphaned). The saga completed partially — a debit without a corresponding credit.
options.feedback: Correct. REGIONAL BY ROW is the key: each row's Raft quorum is determined by its home region's replica placement. A London-homed account row has its quorum in London — 3 London nodes can elect a leaseholder and accept writes without Frankfurt. The CockroachDB documentation explicitly notes that REGIONAL BY ROW trades global consistency for regional availability during partitions. The conflict is not a Raft split-brain — it is a Saga that span the partition boundary, leaving a debit without a credit.

options.label: C
options.text: MirrorMaker 2's bidirectional Kafka replication allowed duplicate payment events to be processed in both regions during the partition, each region crediting the same account.
options.feedback: Kafka MirrorMaker 2 is used for event replication — it does not directly modify account balances. Account balance updates are done by the application reading Kafka events and writing to CockroachDB. MirrorMaker 2 replication lag during the partition would cause delayed processing of Frankfurt events in London (and vice versa) but not direct balance conflicts. The balance conflict arose from the Saga's partial execution at the partition boundary.

options.label: D
options.text: CockroachDB's GLOBAL tables were used for account balances, which allows eventual consistency reads. During the partition, both regions served stale reads that showed different balances.
options.feedback: GLOBAL tables in CockroachDB use optimistic replication and may serve stale reads from local replicas. However, the system description specifies account balances use REGIONAL BY ROW, not GLOBAL. GLOBAL locality is used for payment_transactions (cross-region transfers). The conflict arose specifically because of the in-flight Saga spanning the partition, not from GLOBAL table stale reads.

stages.principalRationale: REGIONAL BY ROW is explicitly an availability-over-consistency trade: each region is autonomous for its home rows. Raft prevents classic split-brain for GLOBAL tables but cannot prevent partial Saga execution when the Saga spans the partition boundary. The CAP theorem applies at the data model level, not just the database level.

stages.question: After the partition heals, how should the 3 accounts with the incomplete Sagas be resolved?

options.label: A
options.text: Let CockroachDB's automatic conflict resolution handle it. CockroachDB uses last-write-wins for conflicting rows.
options.feedback: CockroachDB's last-write-wins MVCC resolution is for conflicts within the CRDT-like REGIONAL BY ROW model — it applies to metadata conflicts, not to business-level financial inconsistencies. A debit of £400 without a corresponding credit is not a database conflict CockroachDB can resolve — it requires business logic to determine whether to: (a) execute the pending credit, (b) reverse the debit, or (c) escalate to manual review.

options.label: B
options.text: Query the Saga event store for all Sagas in PENDING or IN_PROGRESS state at partition time. For each: (a) if both steps (debit and credit) completed successfully on their respective regions — mark COMPLETED; (b) if only step 1 (debit) completed — the Saga is in COMPENSATING state, automatically retry step 2 (Frankfurt credit); (c) if step 2 fails again after retries — trigger compensation (reverse London debit) and alert operations. Never leave a Saga in ambiguous state.
options.feedback: Correct. The Saga event store is the source of truth. Each Saga step is recorded with its outcome — after the partition heals, the Saga orchestrator can query which Sagas were interrupted and determine their resolution path. The key principle: a debit without a credit is a financial emergency that must be automatically compensated or escalated, not left ambiguous. The 3 accounts need explicit resolution, not automatic database conflict resolution.

options.label: C
options.text: Discard all Frankfurt writes from the partition period and replay London's Kafka events to Frankfurt. London was the primary region, so its view is authoritative.
options.feedback: Discarding Frankfurt writes would destroy legitimate Frankfurt-homed account transactions that occurred during the partition. Frankfurt was autonomously serving its local customers correctly during the partition — those are real transactions. There is no basis for treating London as 'authoritative' and Frankfurt as 'secondary' in an active-active architecture.

options.label: D
options.text: Manually review all 3 accounts with the finance team. Determine the correct balance for each and issue adjusting entries via the back-office system.
options.feedback: Manual review is a last resort for the most complex cases. For 3 accounts with identifiable Saga state, automated compensation (using the Saga event store) is faster, more consistent, and creates a proper audit trail. Manual adjusting entries require additional approval workflows and may not create the correct double-entry ledger records. Automated Saga compensation is preferred when the Saga state is clear.

stages.principalRationale: The Saga event store is the source of truth for distributed transaction state. Post-partition recovery is a Saga completion problem, not a database conflict resolution problem. Each incomplete Saga must be driven to completion (or compensation) using the recorded event history.

stages.question: What design change prevents Sagas from being left in inconsistent state during future partitions?

options.label: A
options.text: Move to synchronous replication for all account operations. If Frankfurt is unreachable, London transactions must wait until Frankfurt is available, preventing any partition-era writes.
options.feedback: Synchronous cross-region replication for all account operations would mean a network partition makes both regions unable to serve writes — a complete outage. This trades availability for consistency, which is the opposite of the active-active architecture's design intent. The correct approach is to make Sagas partition-aware, not to eliminate partition tolerance.

options.label: B
options.text: Saga partition awareness: before proceeding to step 2 (cross-region call), the Saga coordinator checks regional connectivity. If Frankfurt is unreachable, the Saga parks in AWAITING_REGION state and does not proceed. When connectivity is restored, the Saga resumes from AWAITING_REGION. Combined with Saga timeout monitoring: any Saga in AWAITING_REGION for > 30 minutes triggers an alert and automatic compensation after a configurable SLA window.
options.feedback: Correct. Saga partition awareness prevents the partial execution scenario: if the Saga detects that the target region is unreachable before step 2, it parks (does not debit) rather than committing step 1 and failing step 2. The AWAITING_REGION state is an explicit, monitored state — not an ambiguous mid-flight failure. When connectivity restores, the Saga resumes cleanly. The timeout-based compensation provides a bounded SLA for transfers: customers are informed within the SLA window whether their transfer will complete or be compensated.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a third region (e.g., Paris) to form a 9-node cluster. The 3-way replication means no single region pair partition can prevent quorum.
options.feedback: A third region increases resilience to 2-node partition scenarios but does not eliminate partition risk. Any 3-node partition that isolates one region still creates the cross-region Saga problem: a Saga step committed in London may fail in Frankfurt if Frankfurt loses its 3 nodes. The fundamental design issue is Sagas spanning partition boundaries — the third region addresses quorum availability but not Saga idempotency across partitions.

options.label: D
options.text: Use 2-Phase Commit instead of Sagas for cross-region transfers. 2PC ensures either both regions commit or neither does.
options.feedback: 2PC across regions is a blocking protocol: if Frankfurt is unavailable, the London coordinator holds its locks and waits indefinitely (or until timeout, causing rollback). This creates the 'London transfers are blocked whenever Frankfurt is degraded' problem — worse availability than the Saga pattern. 2PC is not suitable for cross-region financial transactions due to its blocking nature and lock duration.

stages.principalRationale: Saga partition awareness makes the partition a first-class citizen: Sagas can observe and respond to regional unavailability rather than failing mid-flight. The AWAITING_REGION state is an explicit, bounded, monitored state that can be retried on recovery or compensated on timeout. This is the correct pattern for multi-region financial workflows.

debrief.summary: Active-active multi-region architectures trade global consistency for availability during partitions. REGIONAL BY ROW data models make each region autonomous — which is the feature, not a bug. The design challenge is Sagas that span regions: they must be partition-aware, parking in a safe state when the target region is unreachable, rather than committing step 1 and failing step 2. The Saga event store is the source of truth for post-partition recovery.
keyTakeaways: REGIONAL BY ROW: each region is autonomous for its home rows — intentional AP design for account reads
Raft prevents dual-quorum for GLOBAL tables; REGIONAL BY ROW tables can have per-region quorum
Cross-region Sagas are the highest-risk pattern — they span the partition boundary and can partially commit
Saga partition awareness: check regional connectivity before step 1, park in AWAITING_REGION if unreachable
Post-partition recovery: query Saga event store, complete or compensate each interrupted Saga
